description: Round 1: literature, attack angles, adversarial verification, synthesis (62 agents)

sources.title: Nersissian, 'Diagonal Periods and Newton Supports of Rules 30, 86 and 135', arXiv:2609.25077 (18 Sep 2026, 40 pp.)
sources.what_it_proves: Conventions: b(m,n)=A30(n,n-m+1)=our R_{m-1}(n), and c(t)=b(t+1,t). Right diagonals are written as Newton supports: R_{m-1}(n)=parity #{r in S_m : r is a bitwise subset of n}, with S_1={0}, S_2={1}, S_m=Inc(S_{m-1} Δ S_{m-2} Δ (S_{m-1} ⊛ S_{m-2})), where ⊛ is OR-convolution and Inc shifts by +1. Proved: (1) min S_m = floor(m/2). (2) max S_m <= F_{m+1}-1, via an integer polynomial lift. (3) A finite nonempty S has least period exactly 2^k, where k is minimal with S ⊆ [0,2^k). (4) R_{m-1} is purely periodic with least period 2^{ceil log2(max S_m+1)} >= floor(m/2)+1, and every rise in the running maximum is a doubling. Left side, in the Rule 86 frame where D_m is our D_m: for w(t+1)=u(t) xor (v(t) or w(t)), an active driver (v=1 at some time in the tail) gives period dividing P; an eventually zero driver gives period pi or 2pi according to the parity of u over one period. Also proved: Q_m := max_{j<=m} pi_j = max(pi_{m-1}, pi_m); a record criterion equivalent to Rowland Prop. 2; and a backward-profile pigeonhole bound m+2 <= 4^{Q_m}, so left-diagonal eventual periods are unbounded. Finite certificate only: from a prefix of length 131072, any LSD-first DFAO that outputs c needs at least 8191 states. The paper states explicitly that its fixed-diagonal theorems do not reach the moving center column.
sources.rigor: Rigorous for every theorem listed. I checked the profile pigeonhole proof by hand (zero pair fixed by B, Sigma_0=(0,1), distinctness). I checked the support recurrence, min/max bounds, Lucas evaluation and period law against direct simulation for m<=24 (scripts/check_nersissian.py); |S_20|=105 matches. The proposed next record 2107985256 is explicitly not established. The authors could not reproduce A364239's 87868; our Ruliology data (period 32 first at j=87867) does reproduce it.
sources.relevance: Medium. Gives clean, formalizable tools: the Newton/Lucas formula c(t)=parity #{r in S_{t+1} : r ⊆ t} (only r in [floor((t+1)/2), t] contribute), the reset/integration theorems for the recurrence w(t+1)=u xor (v or w), and a pigeonhole over the backward profile map with a fixed zero boundary. The recurrence has the same form as column -1 driven by c (v=c) and column 1 driven by c (u=c, v=column 2) in our driven-halves framework. No center-column result.

sources.title: Nersissian, 'Diagonal Bases and Diagonal Periods of Elementary Cellular Automata', arXiv:2609.25078 (18 Sep 2026, 44 pp.)
sources.what_it_proves: Mostly classifies which ECA diagonal families form bases (24 rules). For Rule 30 it gives: (1) the telescoped formula R_k(n)=sum_{j<n}(R_{k-1}(j)+R_{k-2}(j)+R_{k-1}(j)R_{k-2}(j)) mod 2 for k>=1, which is the same as our parity identity. (2) Theorem: the integer lift (D_0=1, D_1=t, D_k(t+1)=D_k(t)+D_{k-1}+D_{k-2}+D_{k-1}D_{k-2}) has degree exactly F_{k+2}-1. Corollary: mod any prime p, R_k is purely periodic with period dividing p^{ceil log_p F_{k+2}}. Mod 2 this means period dividing 2^{ceil log2 F_{k+2}}, about 2^{0.694k}, which is sharper than our 2^k. (3) A period-multiplication proposition for left-linear rules mod p. The prize section says no center-column conclusion follows.
sources.rigor: Rigorous (simple degree induction plus Lucas/Frobenius). The degree argument comes from a Mathematica StackExchange answer (q/318912, March 2026).
sources.relevance: Low to medium. It tightens the right-diagonal period bound in Rule30Diagonals.lean from 2^j to 2^{ceil log2 F_{j+2}}. It says nothing about the center column.

sources.title: Chan-López and Martín-Ruiz, 'Symmetric Nonlinear Cellular Automata as Algebraic References for Rule 30', arXiv:2604.00165 (v1 Mar 2026, v3 Sep 2026)
sources.what_it_proves: Rigorous content is about Rule 22: closed form Q_{2j}=(x^2+x^{-2})^j over F2, the support-cardinality formula, and the S3-symmetric and permutive classification (only rules 150 and 105). For Rule 30 it proves only trivial facts: left-permutivity, P(eta_t(0)=1)=1/2 for i.i.d. Bernoulli(1/2) initial data, and that cell -t has influence exactly 1 on eta_t(0). Everything else (deviation ~ m^1.11, sensitivity asymmetry, block entropy up to N=4096, the continuum PDE) is empirical or formal. The conclusion says: 'we obtain no non-periodicity result'.
sources.rigor: Rigorous only for the Rule 22 statements and the trivial Rule 30 facts. The 'mechanism for randomness' is heuristic.
sources.relevance: Very low for Problem 1.

sources.title: Rowland, 'Local Nested Structure in Rule 30', Complex Systems 16(3) (2006) 239-258
sources.what_it_proves: Works with Rule 86 as a range [2,0] right-bijective rule; this is the same computation as rule 30. Prop 1: a rightful row has at most one infinite rightful history. Lemma 1: if R and S first differ at M, then (f^t R)(M) != (f^t S)(M) for every t, forward and backward. Lemma 2: if columns m-d..m-1 are purely periodic, then column m is purely periodic with period dividing l(k)*lcm(...), where l(2)=2. This yields our right diagonals: purely periodic with power-of-2 periods. Theorem 1: f^{l(k)^n} R -> R bitwise, which is the local nested structure at rows 2^n. a(n)=Lambda_I(2^n) is strictly increasing (A094604: 1,3,4,6,7,9,15,16,24,...) and equals the number of right diagonals whose period divides 2^n. Section 5, Prop 2 (Wolfram's NKS p.871 observation, proved for every rightful initial row): left diagonal m doubles its period iff diagonal m-1 is eventually white and diagonal m-2 has an odd number of 1s per period. Lemma 3: a bit at (t0,m) has a long-term effect iff diagonal m-1 is white for t>=t0. Also Conjectures 1-3, and a remark that the left side could first depend on the initial row at column 53209.
sources.rigor: Rigorous for Props 1-2, Lemmas 1-3 and Theorem 1. Conjectures are labeled as such.
sources.relevance: Medium as background. It is the source of the right-side regularity (right bijectivity with a white right tail) and the left-side doubling criterion. Nothing on the center column.

sources.title: Kopra, 'Rapid left expansivity, a commonality between Wolfram's Rule 30 and powers of p/q', Theor. Comput. Sci. 946 (2023) 113668; arXiv:2202.13809
sources.what_it_proves: Defines left expansive CA with dimensions (h,d,w); an (m,n) left-permutive CA is left expansive with (0,1,m+n). Defines left spreading with speed s, and rapid left expansivity (RLE) as s<1/h. Lemma expPer: if the width-w trace at [i,i+w-1] is eventually p-periodic with preperiod c, then the trace at [i-1,i+w-2] is too, with preperiod c+h (h=0 for rule 30). Main theorem: if F is RLE with width w and x is number-like (x != 0 and x_i=0 for i<N), then no width-w trace Tr_{[i,i+w-1]}(x) is eventually periodic. For rule 30, w=2. Two further theorems: F^t(x)|[0,inf) = x|[0,inf) for only finitely many t, and (F^t(x)|[0,inf))_t has infinitely many limit points. Barrier remark: Rule 90 is RLE, yet its single-seed center column is eventually periodic, so width-1 aperiodicity cannot follow from RLE. The width-1 rule-30 question is posed as open (Problem 3.10 in the TCS version).
sources.rigor: Rigorous. The proof generalizes Jen 1990 Prop 3 and is essentially our Rule30Jen argument.
sources.relevance: High as context and for generalizing: it extends our Lean Jen theorem from the seed to every left-bounded nonzero configuration, including ones with infinite support on the right. That matters if the driven-halves or absorbing-word arguments need Jen for arbitrary right halves. It also defines the barrier any proof must get past.

sources.title: Condrey, 'Finite Configurations Cannot Generate a Constant Trace in Rule 30', arXiv:2609.09431 (8 Sep 2026); ancillary Rule30ZeroTail.lean and Python probes
sources.what_it_proves: Notation: c_t=F^t(x)_0, R_j=x_j, L_j=x_{-j}. Lemma (triangular uniqueness): two configurations equal on [0,inf) with equal center traces are equal. Finite form: if traces agree on [0,r], the configurations agree on [-r,-1]. Thm (zero-trace fiber): if R_0=0 and the first right 1 is at m, the unique left half with an all-zero trace is L_j=0 for j<m, L_m=1, L_j=j mod 2 for j>m. Prefix-OR form: L_{2k+1}=OR_{j<=2k+1} R_j and L_{2k}=R_{2k} AND NOT OR_{j<2k} R_j. Thm (all-one fiber): if R_0=1, then L_j=1 iff j is positive and even, the same for every right half. Corollary: no column of the orbit of any nonzero finite configuration is eventually constant. Sharp horizons: for support radius w the longest constant prefix is w+2, and the paper counts the extremizers. Remark: H(2,w)>=w, so there is no bounded-horizon law for period 2; eventual period 2 is named the next open case. The ancillary probe also checks a 'time-shift defect identity': if c(t)=c(t+P) and c(t+1)=c(t+1+P), then cell(t+P,-1) xor cell(t,-1) = (NOT c(t)) AND (cell(t+P,1) xor cell(t,1)).
sources.rigor: Rigorous and elementary. I verified both fibers numerically on 300 random right halves inside the light cone (scripts/check_condrey.py), and the defect identity is a two-line derivation. Per its own appendix, the Lean ancillary is partial: it does not derive the classification from an all-zero trace and does not cover the one-fiber or the horizons. I did not run or compile the downloaded code.
sources.relevance: High: this is the frontier result. Our Lean already has period 1 for the seed; Condrey extends it to every finite configuration and makes period 2 the explicit open frontier. Its methods (left-permutive triangular uniqueness, plus the rule-30-specific OR latch R'_1 = 1 OR R_2 = 1) are the natural tools for attempting period 2.

sources.title: Jen, 'Aperiodicity in one-dimensional cellular automata', Physica D 45 (1990) 3-18 (LANL preprint LA-UR-90-761)
sources.what_it_proves: Lemma: if columns i<j are eventually periodic, every column between them is eventually periodic with period dividing lcm and a uniformly bounded transient. Prop 3: if the rule is injective in the (i-1) component and 001->1 (Jen lists 30, 86, 90, 150, 210 among such rules), then any finite initial condition has at most one eventually periodic column. Prop 2: Rule 90's temporal sequences are aperiodic except in a trivial symmetric case. Also a linearization technique for Rule 18.
sources.rigor: Rigorous (classical). I read it from an OCR'd preprint, not the journal version.
sources.relevance: Already formalized (Rule30Jen.lean). Jen's own list of qualifying rules contains 90, 150 and 210, whose single-seed centers are eventually periodic (see the barrier theorem).

sources.title: Jen, 'Global properties of cellular automata', J. Stat. Phys. 43 (1986) 219-242
sources.what_it_proves: As cited by Condrey and Rowland (I did not read the paywalled text): Thm 2b, a finite rule-30 orbit has at most one eventually periodic column; Thm 4, columns of range [d,0] CA from rightful initial conditions are eventually periodic, which gives eventual periodicity of the left diagonals; Thm 7a, necessary and sufficient conditions for a finite initial condition to produce an eventually-one temporal sequence, which already excludes eventually-1 columns for finite rule-30 configurations.
sources.rigor: Peer-reviewed classical result; statements here are second-hand.
sources.relevance: Background, already used.

sources.title: Coven, Pivato, Yassawi, 'Prevalence of odometers in cellular automata', Proc. AMS 135 (2007) 815-821; arXiv:math/0511030
sources.what_it_proves: Thm: let Phi be left permutive with no memory. If x's right half is fixed by the one-sided map Phi_R and the orbit is infinite, then Phi on the orbit closure of x is topologically conjugate to an odometer, (s_i)-adic with s_i <= alphabet size. Applied to rule 30 in the diagonal frame y_t(i)=cell(t,t+i), local rule a xor (b or c), with seed delta_0: Phi on the orbit closure is conjugate to the 2-adic odometer, i.e. n -> F^n(delta) is a 2-adically uniformly continuous bijection onto a dense subset.
sources.rigor: Rigorous; the rule-30 specialization is my direct application of their theorem.
sources.relevance: Low to medium. It is a clean structural reformulation: c(t)=y_t(-t) reads the 2-adic odometer orbit at a moving coordinate. It explains why fixed-diagonal and fixed-window techniques do not reach c, but it gives no new constraint.

sources.title: Brunnbauer, 'Diagonals in elementary cellular automaton 30' (web note, 2019; PDF copy at OEIS A364239)
sources.what_it_proves: Gives an integer polynomial lift of the right and left diagonals and an intersection identity between them. States the right-diagonal doubling criterion: the period doubles iff the OR-input has odd parity over its period, and a doubled period word has the form A·complement(A). Argues eventual periodicity of the left diagonals by a finite-state argument. Sketches, via trailing zeros, that right-diagonal periods never decrease.
sources.rigor: The summation/doubling lemma is rigorous. The monotonicity of right periods is only a 'proof idea', not established. The author calls it amateur work.
sources.relevance: Low. The doubling criterion is the same as Nersissian's parity theorem.

sources.title: OEIS A094605, A094604, A094606, A363345, A363346, A364239, A364773, A328100-A328102
sources.what_it_proves: Data: right-diagonal periods (A094605) and a(n) (A094604, extended to a(57) in Aug 2026); left eventual periods and transients (A363345, A363346); left record indices 1,4,9,30,401,87868 (A364239); right period words (A364773); neighbor columns of the center (A328100-A328102).
sources.rigor: Computed data.
sources.relevance: Low. They are cross-checks for the brief's e_j and left-diagonal data, which agree.

sources.title: Wolfram, 'Announcing the Rule 30 Prizes' (Oct 2019)
sources.what_it_proves: Gives the official problem statements. Credits Jen with the two-column result. Says, with no reference, that 'one can also give arguments that a single column plus scattered cells in another column can't both be periodic' and that the argument works 'if one doesn't know every cell'. Empirical claims: the order/disorder boundary moves left about 0.252 cells per step over roughly 1e5 steps; finite-ring periods are about 2^{0.63n}. Also notes that an affirmative Problem 3 implies an affirmative Problem 1, and diagonals at 45° are periodic.
sources.rigor: Expository; no proofs. The 'scattered cells' claim has no precise statement or reference.
sources.relevance: Low. One point worth checking: c alone already fixes column -1 at every time with c(t)=1, since cell(t,-1) = NOT c(t+1) there, so 'scattered cells' of that kind come for free and cannot give a contradiction by themselves.

sources.title: Das, 'Rule 30: Solving the Chaos', arXiv:2207.13237 (2022)
sources.what_it_proves: Nothing rigorous. It argues from a simulated 'randomness count' (about 0.14) that the center column is random and therefore aperiodic.
sources.rigor: Heuristic and empirical; not a proof.
sources.relevance: None (claimed solution, invalid).

sources.title: Fradkin, 'Rule 30 Resolved: Synchronization, Uniform Cylinder Frequencies, and Unconditional Convergence from First Principles', Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.18838239 (Mar 2026)
sources.what_it_proves: Nothing verifiable; it is an 'energetic framework' with asserted stability and spectral-gap conditions.
sources.rigor: Not a proof (only the landing page was inspected).
sources.relevance: None.

sources.title: Natal and Al-saadi, 'Fast Simulation of Cellular Automata by Self-Composition', arXiv:2409.07065 (2024)
sources.what_it_proves: Computes generation n of a CA in O(n^2/log n) time by composing the rule.
sources.rigor: Algorithmic.
sources.relevance: None for Problem 1; tangential to Problem 3.

sources.title: Cappallo, 'Any example of periodic columns in asymmetrical 1D cellular automata?' (Wolfram Community, 2021)
sources.what_it_proves: Only asks whether an asymmetric rule has an isolated periodic column; no results. The question bears on the barrier: Rule 210 is asymmetric, and its single-seed center column is eventually 0, though only because its seed orbit coincides with Rule 90's.
sources.rigor: Question only.
sources.relevance: Low.

useful_theorems: [Kopra 2023, Lemma expPer plus main theorem, rule 30 case h=0, w=2] Let x != 0 with x_i=0 for all i<N. For every i, t -> (F^t x)_i, (F^t x)_{i+1} is not eventually periodic. Step lemma: if columns i and i+1 are p-periodic for t>=c, then column i-1 is p-periodic for t>=c, because cell(t,i-1)=cell(t+1,i) xor (cell(t,i) or cell(t,i+1)). This generalizes Rule30Jen.lean from the seed to every left-bounded nonzero configuration.

[Kopra 2023 barrier, sharpened and verified by me] The ECAs that are left-permutive (f=p xor h(q,r)), quiescent (h(0,0)=0) and left-spreading (h(0,1)=1) are exactly rules 30 (h=q or r), 90 (h=r), 150 (h=q xor r) and 210 (h=(not q) and r). Their single-seed center columns: Rule 90 gives 1,0,0,..., since C(2k,k) is even for k>=1. Rule 150 is constantly 1: the central trinomial coefficient is sum_a C(t,2a)C(2a,a), which is 1 mod 2. Rule 210 gives 1,0,0,...: Rule 210 = Rule 90 xor qr, and Rule 90's seed orbit never has two adjacent 1s, so the two seed orbits coincide. I checked this for 600 to 2000 steps (scripts/barrier_rules.py, scripts/rule210_vs_90.py). Consequence: an argument that applies uniformly to rules and uses only left-permutivity, quiescence, f(001)=1, and one of h(1,0)=1, h(1,1)=1 or nonlinearity cannot prove Problem 1, because it would also cover rule 150, 90 or 210. Any proof must use h(1,0)=h(1,1)=1 together, i.e. the full OR (the latch 'cell(t,p)=1 implies cell(t+1,p) = NOT cell(t,p-1)').

[Condrey 2026, triangular uniqueness] If x and y agree on [0,inf) and F^t(x)_0 = F^t(y)_0 for 0<=t<=r, then x and y agree on [-r,-1]. The infinite version says the right half plus the center trace determine the left half. This is the rigorous form of the brief's driven-halves consistency.

[Condrey 2026, constant fibers] If x_0=0 and the first right 1 is at m>=1, the all-zero trace forces L_j=0 for j<m, L_m=1, and L_j=j mod 2 for j>m. The invariant classes C_m satisfy F(C_m) ⊆ C_{m-1} and F(C_1) ⊆ C_1. If x_0=1, the all-one trace forces L_j=1 iff j is positive and even. Corollary: no column of a nonzero finite orbit is eventually constant. Sharp horizon: for support radius w the longest constant center prefix has length w+2. Remark: for period 2 the realizable prefix length is at least w for every w, so finite-horizon certificates cannot exclude period 2 without seed-specific input.

[Time-shift defect identity; Condrey ancillary, two-line proof] Write d_p(t) = cell(t+P,p) xor cell(t,p). If c(t)=c(t+P) and c(t+1)=c(t+1+P), then d_{-1}(t) = (NOT c(t)) AND d_1(t). Equivalently: whenever c(t)=1, cell(t,-1) = NOT c(t+1) is fixed by c alone. So if c is eventually P-periodic from T, column -1 is automatically P-periodic on {t>=T : c(t)=1}. Combined with Jen/Kopra (columns 0 and ±1 are not both eventually periodic), there are infinitely many t>=T with c(t)=0 and d_{-1}(t)=d_1(t)=1. For period 2 with c alternating from T: cell(t,-1)=1 and cell(t,-2)=cell(t+1,-2) = NOT cell(t+1,-1) whenever c(t)=1. This is my own derivation from the rule.

[Nersissian 2026a, Newton supports] R_{m-1}(n) = parity #{r in S_m : (r AND n) = r}, with S_1={0}, S_2={1}, S_m = Inc(S_{m-1} Δ S_{m-2} Δ (S_{m-1} ⊛ S_{m-2})). Also min S_m = floor(m/2) and max S_m <= F_{m+1}-1, and the least period of R_{m-1} is 2^{bitlength(max S_m)}. Hence c(t) = parity #{r in S_{t+1} : r ⊆ t bitwise}, where only r in [floor((t+1)/2), t] contribute. I verified this for m<=24 against simulation.

[Nersissian 2026b, Fibonacci period bound] The integer lift of R_k has degree exactly F_{k+2}-1, so the least period of R_k divides 2^{ceil(log2 F_{k+2})}, about 2^{0.694k}. This improves Rule30Diagonals.lean's 2^k. The observed e_k/k is about 0.43.

[Nersissian 2026a, reset/integration for w(t+1) = u(t) xor (v(t) or w(t))] Suppose u and v are eventually periodic with common period P. If v(t0)=1 at some t0 past the transient, then w is eventually P-periodic (reset). If v is eventually 0, the least period of w is pi or 2pi according to the parity of u over one period pi (integration), and the record criterion follows. The same recurrence describes the left diagonals (u=D_{m-2}, v=D_{m-1}), column -1 driven by c (v=c, u=column -2), and column 1 driven by c (u=c, v=column 2).

[Nersissian 2026a, backward-profile pigeonhole] Let Q_m = max_{j<=m} (least eventual period of D_j). Then m+2 <= 4^{Q_m}. Proof: B(u,v) = (t -> v(t+1) xor (u(t) or v(t)), u) on pairs of Q_m-periodic profiles maps Sigma_j=(p_{j-1},p_j) to Sigma_{j-1}. The pair (0,0)=Sigma_{-1} is fixed, and Sigma_0=(0,1) differs from it, so Sigma_{-1},...,Sigma_m are distinct. Also Q_m = max(pi_{m-1}, pi_m). This is formalizable and gives unbounded left-diagonal periods.

[Rowland 2006, Prop 2] For rule 30 started from any row that is 0 far to the left, left diagonal m doubles its eventual period iff diagonal m-1 is eventually 0 and diagonal m-2 has odd parity per period. Lemma 3: information at (t0, diagonal m) persists iff diagonal m-1 is 0 for all t>=t0.

[Rowland 2006, Lemma 2 and Theorem 1] For right-bijective range [d,0] rules (rule 30 seen along right diagonals), purely periodic columns m-d..m-1 force column m to be purely periodic with period dividing 2*lcm. Also f^{2^n}(I) -> I bitwise, and a(n) = #{j : e_j <= n} is strictly increasing (A094604).

[Coven-Pivato-Yassawi 2007, applied to rule 30] In the diagonal frame y_t(i)=cell(t,t+i), rule 30 restricted to the orbit closure of the seed is conjugate to the 2-adic odometer. So c(t)=y_t(-t) is a moving-coordinate readout of an odometer, and there is no fixed-coordinate (continuous) description of c.

[Jen 1990, Lemma] Two eventually periodic columns i<j force every column between them to be eventually periodic with period dividing lcm(p_i,p_j) and a uniformly bounded transient. Prop 3: rules injective in the left argument with 001->1 have at most one eventually periodic column from any finite initial condition.

[My computation, evidence only] No nonzero finite rule-30 configuration with support in [-9,9] (all 524,287) has a center column periodic with any period p<=512 on t in [1024,2048) (scripts/finite_configs.c). This is consistent with the open finite-configuration version of Problem 1, which Kopra's thesis records as open.
result.summary:
Problem 1 is still open as of Oct 2026, and none of the papers claims otherwise. Nersissian 2609.25077 and Chan-López/Martín-Ruiz 2604.00165 say explicitly that their results do not reach the center column, and Condrey 2609.09431 names eventual period 2 as the next open case.

**What is rigorous and usable:**
1. **Two columns.** Jen 1986/1990 and Kopra (TCS 2023) show that no width-2 trace is eventually periodic. Kopra's version holds for every nonzero configuration that is 0 far to the left, not just the seed. That would extend our Lean Jen theorem if the driven-halves argument needs Jen for arbitrary right halves.
2. **Period 1 for all finite configurations.** Condrey 2026 classifies exactly which left halves give a constant trace and proves no nonzero finite orbit has an eventually constant column. His tools (the left half is determined by the right half plus the trace, and the OR latch) are the natural starting point for period 2. He also observes that finite-window certificates alone cannot exclude period 2.
3. **Diagonals only.** Nersissian 2026 proves:
   - the Newton-support and Lucas formula for the right diagonals, which also gives c(t) = parity #{r in S_{t+1} : r ⊆ t};
   - first-contact and Fibonacci bounds on those supports, the exact power-of-2 period law, and a sharper right-diagonal period bound 2^{ceil log2 F_{j+2}};
   - reset/integration theorems for the recurrence w(t+1) = u xor (v or w);
   - a pigeonhole argument showing left-diagonal periods are unbounded (Q_m >= ½ log2(m+2)).
   
   Rowland 2006 proves the right-side nested structure and the left-side period-doubling criterion.
4. **Odometer form.** In the diagonal frame, rule 30 on the seed's orbit closure is the 2-adic odometer (Coven–Pivato–Yassawi). So c is a moving-coordinate readout of an odometer.

**Barrier.** The ECAs that are left-permutive, quiescent and have f(001)=1 are exactly rules 30, 90, 150 and 210. Rules 90 (1,0,0,…), 150 (all 1s) and 210 (same seed orbit as Rule 90) all have eventually periodic single-seed centers. I proved this and checked it numerically. So a proof must use the full OR (h(1,0) = h(1,1) = 1); left-permutivity, nonlinearity, or one of those two values alone is not enough.

**An elementary tool.** If c is P-periodic at t and t+1, then cell(t+P,−1) xor cell(t,−1) = (NOT c(t)) AND (cell(t+P,1) xor cell(t,1)). In particular c alone fixes column −1 wherever c=1. So under eventual periodicity, the aperiodicity that Jen/Kopra force must sit at times where c=0, and appears in columns −1 and +1 at the same moments.

**Checks I ran:**
- Nersissian's support facts match simulation for m ≤ 24.
- Condrey's two fibers hold on 300 random right halves.
- No nonzero finite configuration with support in [−9,9] (524,287 of them) has a center column periodic with period ≤ 512 on t in [1024, 2048). This is evidence only.

**For the Lean effort:**
- Strengthen Jen to all left-bounded configurations (Kopra).
- Formalize Condrey's fibers and the uniqueness lemma as a base for period 2.
- Optionally add the Fibonacci period bound and the left-diagonal pigeonhole.

None of these closes the single-column gap.

Notes and scripts are in /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30prize/lit-recent/ (NOTES.txt; scripts/barrier_rules.py, rule210_vs_90.py, check_nersissian.py, check_condrey.py, finite_configs.c). Downloaded sources are in the dl_* subfolders there, and I treated them as read-only data.
result.claimed_solutions_assessment:
No valid solution exists in the literature as of 2026-10-15.

- **Das, arXiv 2207.13237 (2022)** claims an 'analytical solution'. Its argument: a simulated 'randomness count' of about 0.14 is nonzero, so the column is 'random', so it is aperiodic. That is heuristic. An eventually periodic sequence can have any density of (1,1) neighbourhoods, so it proves nothing.
- **Fradkin, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.18838239 (2026), 'Rule 30 Resolved'** is an 'energetic framework' with asserted stability and spectral-gap conditions and no verifiable derivation. Not a proof (I inspected only the record page).
- **Brauer (2025)** is statistics only (symbolic drift, an FSM over 3-bit states) and claims no proof.
- **Chan-López and Martín-Ruiz (2604.00165)** say explicitly that they obtain no non-periodicity result. Their randomness 'mechanism' is heuristic.
- **Nersissian (2609.25077/25078)** says explicitly that the fixed-diagonal theorems do not determine the center column. Their 8191-state DFAO bound is only a finite certificate.
- **Condrey (2609.09431)** proves only the eventually-constant case, for every finite configuration, and states that every nonconstant period, including period 2, is open.
- **Wolfram's 2019 'single column plus scattered cells' claim** has no precise statement or reference. The cells that c already determines (column −1 wherever c=1) give no contradiction by themselves.

result.summary:
Bottom line (checked 2026-10-15): none of the claimed solutions holds up, and all three Rule 30 Prizes are officially open.

OFFICIAL STATUS. rule30prize.org, fetched today:
- It lists three $10,000 problems and says submissions are accepted "until a satisfactory Solution has been achieved".
- It names no winners and recognizes no partial results.
- Its bibliography stops at 2019. Kopra 2023, Condrey 2026 and the other newer work are not listed.

Wolfram's 2019 announcement is the only official discussion of progress. It says:
- the column is known non-periodic for the first 10^9 steps (by computation only);
- Jen (1986) showed no two columns can both become periodic;
- "arguments" exist that a column plus scattered cells of another column cannot both be periodic;
- getting the effort below O(n^2) "would be a nice partial result".

Problem 3 has a wording gap. The prose asks for "at least O(n)" effort. The formal statement literally says no finite machine m computes c(n) with lim sup effort(n)/n < infinity.

On the Wolfram Community thread "Wolfram's Rule 30 contest":
- users asked in October 2024 and February 2026 whether the prize is still running, and no staff member answered;
- T. Nersissian reports submitting through the official form around 2026-01-17 and receiving no confirmation.

CLAIMED SOLUTIONS. All are invalid; details are in claimed_solutions_assessment. Each has a concrete fatal gap, and most "prove too much": the same argument would prove something false for another rule or another initial condition.
- Das 2022 (arXiv 2207.13237)
- Basta 2025 (ResearchGate, BHLM-Bas-Zeta)
- Fradkin 2026 (Zenodo 18838239, 166 pages)
- Brauer 2025 (Zenodo 16730084)
- Deva 2025/26 (SSRN 5908722; only the abstract could be read)
- Tan Kian Cheng 2026. Titled a "Resolution", but it only contains simulation code.
- viXra: its site search finds no Rule 30 prize claims.
- Some tracking pages that search engines still index now return 404: the GitHub repo dcondrey/rule30 and issues in woahwhattheheck/commons.

RIGOROUS FRONTIER FOR PROBLEM 1.
- Jen 1986/1990: no two adjacent columns are both eventually periodic, and a finite orbit has at most one eventually periodic column.
- Kopra (TCS 2023): extends this to a whole class of rules ("rapidly left expansive"); his Problem 4.8 is exactly Prize Problem 1.
- Condrey (arXiv 2609.09431, Sept 2026): the period-1 case for every nonzero finite configuration. This is the general form of our Lean "no column eventually constant". He states period 2 is the next open case.
- Nersissian (arXiv 2609.25077): fixed-diagonal periods are unbounded; this does not address the center column.

BARRIERS this survey makes explicit:
- (a) Rule 30 itself has initial conditions with a constant center trace: Condrey's checkerboard left half has center ≡ 1, and his alternating tails give center ≡ 0. So no argument that uses only the local rule can work: not left-permutivity, not algebraic-degree or decision-tree bounds for the n-step map, not truth-table balance. A proof must use finiteness of the seed's support or similar seed-specific facts.
- (b) Rule 90 is left-permutive and rapidly left expansive, yet its single-seed center column is 1,0,0,… (Kopra's remark).
- (c) Rule 30 on finite rings has every column eventually periodic, yet nonlinear "branching" stays frequent and the bit density is about 1/2.
- (d) Condrey shows that for period 2, finite rows of radius about N can reproduce any trace prefix of length N. Bounded-horizon or "window" methods therefore cannot exclude period 2 by themselves.

LOCAL ARTIFACTS (all under /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30prize/literature/):
- Extracted texts: das2022.txt, condrey2026.txt, kopra2022.txt, brauer2025.txt, fradkin2026.txt, nersissian2026a.txt.
- Checks in scripts/:
  - check_condrey.py: confirms Condrey's Theorems 2 and 3 and his horizon table for w ≤ 7.
  - anf_degree.py: algebraic degree of the n-step center map is 2,3,5,7,9,11 for Rule 30 and 2n+1 for Rule 22 (n ≤ 6). Single-seed center columns: Rule 22 and Rule 18 are eventually 0, Rule 150 is all 1s, Rule 90 is 1,0,0,….
  - ring_branching.py: Rule 30 on rings of size 5 to 25.
- The Basta full text was read in the browser through ResearchGate's reader. The SSRN full text was not read because SSRN shows a human-verification (Cloudflare) check, which I did not try to get past.
result.claimed_solutions_assessment:
Each entry gives the claimed theorem, the key argument, and the fatal gap.

1. Das, "Rule 30: Solving the Chaos", arXiv 2207.13237v1 (27 Jul 2022; 3 pages; primary class cs.CG; never revised).
- CLAIM: an "analytical solution" to Problem 1 (Section 5, "Conclusion to Problem 1": the center column "will always be aperiodic").
- ARGUMENT:
  - Rule 30 differs from Rule 150 only when center = right = 1 ("decisive branching").
  - The "randomness count" (the fraction of updates where center = right = 1) settles near 0.14 up to 16,384 steps.
  - It has Pearson correlation 0.45 with the 0/1 ratio of the center column, and "correlation equals causation".
  - The ratio is about 1 in 10^9 bits, so the count never reaches 0, so the column is "purely random", hence aperiodic.
- FATAL GAPS:
  - (i) Every step is finite numerics or analogy. Nothing is defined, no limit is proved, and "random" is never defined.
  - (ii) The core inference "branching occurs with positive frequency ⇒ center column aperiodic" is false. Rule 30 on cyclic lattices of size 5 to 25 (my run, ring_branching.py) has every column eventually periodic. Yet the branching fraction on the cycle is 0.24 to 0.40 and the center density is about 0.5.
  - (iii) The premise "0/1 ratio → 1" is itself the open Problem 2. Even if granted, it does not rule out periodicity: (01)^∞ has ratio 1.
  - (iv) Factual error: "Rule 30 AND Rule 150" is Rule 22, not Rule 90 (Fig. 6).

2. Basta, "BHLM–Bas–Zeta Wolfram Project: Formal Resolutions of Wolfram-Family Open Problems" (ResearchGate, Nov 2025; DOI 10.13140/RG.2.2.12615.15528; 15 pages).
- CLAIMS: Problems 1, 2 and 3, plus "resolutions" of three Wolfram Physics Project questions (emergent spacetime, Einstein's equations, quantum interference).
- Problem 1 argument:
  - It defines ε_k(C_k) = C_k·λ_{α,k}·k^{αδ}.
  - Step 3 says eventual periodicity C_n = C_{n+p} gives ε_n(C_n) = ε_{n+p}(C_{n+p}), "however" these differ because of the factor k^{αδ}, "contradiction".
  - FATAL GAP: ε depends explicitly on the index k, so periodicity of C does not imply periodicity of ε. The contradiction is manufactured.
  - The argument applies word for word to any eventually periodic sequence with infinitely many 1s. Example: the single-seed center column of Rule 150 is identically 1, because central trinomial coefficients are all odd (also checked to t = 60).
  - The theorem's own condition ("spectral novelty") holds for the constant sequence 1,1,1,… when λ is constant. Terms such as "governed integral", "BHLM set theory" and "governed spectral evolution" are never defined.
- Problem 2:
  - Step 3 "invokes the Bas–Zeta epsilon-class irreducibility postulate: Σ C_k ~ n/2 + o(n)". That is the statement to be proved, assumed outright (circular).
  - The proof's own P_n = ΣC_kμ(k)/Σμ(k), with μ(k) = C_k·e^{…}, equals 1 identically because C_k² = C_k. This contradicts the claimed limit 1/2.
  - With σ fixed, the Gaussian sums stay bounded rather than growing like c·n.
- Problem 3:
  - It lower-bounds an arbitrary "spectral path integral" Σε_k, which has no relation to the running time of any machine.
  - "Governed evolution forbids skipping" is an assumption, not a proof.
  - The argument would equally "prove" that Rule 150's all-ones center column takes Ω(n) effort.

3. Fradkin, "Rule 30 Resolved: Synchronization, Uniform Cylinder Frequencies, and Unconditional Convergence from First Principles" (Zenodo 18838239, 2 Mar 2026; a 166-page series of 34 Parts dated from Oct 2025).
- CLAIMS: Problem 1 (Part 4, Corollary 7.1 "Problem 1 resolved"; details in Part 8, Theorem 5.1), Problem 2 (Parts 5 and 15–34, an "unconditional main theorem"), and Problem 3 (Parts 6–7).
- Problem 1:
  - ARGUMENT: for every M, build y(M) that equals the seed on [−M, M]. Then choose cells outside [−M, M] (within distance n of the origin, with M ≪ n) and right-boundary bits so that c(t) ≠ c(t+p) at some t in [n/3, 2n/3]. Conclude: "as M → ∞, locality implies the genuine seed center also violates period p".
  - FATAL GAP: the violating time t ≥ n/3 is far larger than M. The violation depends on exactly the cells where y(M) differs from the seed, and the witness time escapes to infinity.
  - The set P(p,T) of configurations whose center column is p-periodic from time T is closed. A limit of points outside a closed set can lie inside it, so the conclusion does not follow.
  - The argument uses only left-permutivity, so it applies word for word to Rule 90, whose single-seed center column 1,0,0,… is eventually periodic. It proves a falsehood.
  - The statements in Part 4 that aperiodicity holds for a "residual" (topologically generic) set and for almost every random Bernoulli initial condition are true but irrelevant to the seed.
- Problem 2:
  - Part 5 proves the 1/2 frequency only for random Bernoulli(1/2) initial data. That is true and easy, because the center trace of a left-permutive rule is then i.i.d. uniform.
  - Its Theorem 7.1 ("residual half-frequency") is false. The trace map is continuous and open, and the set of sequences with frequency 1/2 is meagre, so the set of initial conditions whose trace has frequency 1/2 is meagre, not residual (my derivation).
  - The seed route rests on Part 20 (Lemma 4.1 and Theorems 5.1/6.1). It applies Birkhoff genericity of a fixed point ζ to hand-picked times s_t, chosen as occurrences of the seed's own words. That is circular, and the theorem is false.
  - Counterexample: take any sequence whose orbit closure is the full shift but whose density of 1s tends to 0 (long runs of 0s interleaved with a density-zero listing of all words; marker m = 11111; η* uniform Bernoulli; ζ normal). It satisfies Assumptions 2.1–2.4 but violates the conclusion.
  - Part 21 also swaps between two different measures. One has mean 1/2 (built in Part 15); the other is supported on the seed's orbit closure Ω. Route B would need every positive-measure word to appear in the seed's column, which is itself open.
- Problem 3 (Parts 6–7):
  - The lower bounds are for f_n(u), the center bit after n steps as a function of an arbitrary window u of 2n+1 initial bits. The prize asks about the single fixed seed, where the input is just n.
  - The key lemmas fail already at n = 1. Part 6 Lemma 2.1/3.1 ("both outputs remain feasible for any strict partial assignment") and Part 7 Theorem 2.1(a) ("conditional error exactly 1/2 at every shallow leaf") are both false: u_{−1} = 0, u_0 = 1 forces f_1 = 1.
- Other errors: Part 2 says Rule 30 is not surjective (false; left-permutive rules are surjective). Part 2 Lemma 3.1 claims a bijection {0,1}^n → {0,1}^{|B|} with |B| < n.

4. Brauer, "Statistical Randomness in the Central Column of Rule 30" (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.16730084; GitHub lba-brauer/rule30-symbolic-fsm; Aug 2025; 11 pages).
- CLAIMS: the README marks Q1, Q2 and Q3 as solved, via Theorems 4.1, 5.2 and 5.1. Each comes with a "Justification" rather than a proof.
- Theorem 4.1 (non-periodicity): the "FSM" is the 8-state map (x,y,z) → (y,z,x⊕(y∨z)), a shift register and not the cellular automaton. Its cycles have lengths 1, 2 and 5, and every orbit of a deterministic 8-state map is eventually periodic. So the center column is not an orbit of it. The claim rests on 200-step entropy estimates.
- Theorem 5.2 (bit balance): "the rule's truth table is balanced" plus "if windows were uniform", plus 200 steps of data. This assumes the conclusion. The same rule gives center ≡ 1 from Condrey's checkerboard initial condition.
- Theorem 5.1 (Ω(n) effort): "a dependency cone of width 2n+1 forces unfolding". This fails for Rule 150, which has the same cone but an all-ones center column computable in O(1). No model of computation is specified.

5. Deva, "Algebraic Obstruction and Dual-Flow Consistency in Rule 30" (SSRN 5908722, Dec 2025 / Jan 2026). FULL TEXT NOT READ: SSRN shows a human-verification check, which I did not try to get past. Only the abstract, via search snippets, and an informal GitHub audit (PR #15682 in woahwhattheheck/commons, also now 404) were seen.
- CLAIMS:
  - linear growth in the algebraic degree of the n-step center function, plus "algebraic immunity" and "essential-variable saturation", give an Ω(n) decision-tree lower bound for the n-th center bit;
  - unbounded degree growth rules out any finite linear recurrence, hence non-periodicity.
- GAP, as stated in the abstract:
  - Degree and decision-tree depth are properties of f_n as a function of all 2n+1 initial bits. The prize concerns one input, the seed.
  - Rigorous counterexample inside Rule 30: Condrey's checkerboard configuration (x_0 = 1, x_{−j} = 1 exactly for positive even j, any right half) uses the same f_n but has center ≡ 1. Degree and decision-tree bounds therefore imply neither non-periodicity nor Ω(n) cost for a specific trace.
  - Illustration: Rule 22 has the maximal possible degree 2n+1 for n ≤ 6 (my computation), yet its single-seed center column is 1,1,0,0,….
  - The degree claim for Rule 30 itself (2n−1 for 2 ≤ n ≤ 6 by my computation) is plausible but irrelevant.
  - This verdict should be re-checked if the full text uses seed-specific facts.

6. Tan Kian Cheng, "Wolfram-Rule30-Resolution" (GitHub tankiancheng1974-SGP; Zenodo 22876299; Sept 2026). No theorem about any prize problem. The content is the standard bitwise simulation Next = (V<<1) ^ (V | (V>>1)), checked for 20 generations, plus narrative.

7. Nersissian. Wolfram Community posts of 12 Feb and 2 Mar 2026 (the latter marked a Staff Pick), a reported prize-form submission around 17 Jan 2026 with no public outcome, and arXiv 2609.25077 / 2609.25078 (Sept 2026).
- The public arXiv versions do not claim Problem 1; they say the diagonal theorems do not determine the eventual behaviour of the center column.
- The community post's "Zeta-Floor reduction" is presented as isolating the open problem, not solving it. Its "fast evaluation" uses "supplied representations" whose construction cost is not bounded, so it has no bearing on Problem 3.
- Genuine content: Theorem 8 below, which is correct and elementary.

8. Not claims of a solution, but checked:
- Condrey, arXiv 2609.09431: rigorous partial result, explicitly not a prize claim. I found no gap, and its theorems and table check out numerically.
- Kopra, TCS 946 (2023): peer-reviewed and rigorous.
- Chan-López and Martín-Ruiz, arXiv 2604.00165: proves a closed form for Rule 22; its Rule 30 material is empirical or heuristic and makes no prize claim.
- Natal and Al-saadi, arXiv 2409.07065: a generic O(n²/log n) simulation speedup; not a prize result.

sources.title: Das, 'Rule 30: Solving the Chaos' (arXiv 2207.13237v1, 2022)
sources.what_it_proves: Nothing rigorous. Claims Problem 1 from empirical 'randomness count' (center=right=1 frequency ≈0.14 up to 16384 steps), a 0.45 correlation and 'correlation equals causation'.
sources.rigor: Invalid. Purely empirical, with a false core inference: Rule 30 on rings has periodic columns despite about 25% branching and density about 0.5. Also mislabels Rule 22 as Rule 90.
sources.relevance: One of the two named targets; refuted.

sources.what_it_proves: Nothing. Claims Problems 1–3 plus Wolfram Physics Project results using undefined 'epsilon-class / governed integral' notions.
sources.rigor: Invalid. Problem 1: an index-dependent encoding makes every periodic sequence with infinitely many 1s 'non-periodic' (refuted by Rule 150's all-ones center column). Problem 2: assumes Σ C_k ~ n/2 as a 'postulate', and the proof's own P_n is identically 1. Problem 3: no computational model.

sources.title: Fradkin, 'Rule 30 Resolved: Synchronization, Uniform Cylinder Frequencies, and Unconditional Convergence from First Principles' (Zenodo 18838239, 2026; 166 pp.)
sources.what_it_proves: True but known or easy: Rule 30 is topologically mixing; the center trace is aperiodic for generic (residual) and Bernoulli-random initial conditions; frequency 1/2 under Bernoulli(1/2) initial data. Its claims about the seed are not proved.
sources.rigor: Invalid for all three prizes. Problem 1: a limit argument whose witness times escape to infinity; it also 'proves' a falsehood for Rule 90. Problem 2: Part 20 UCF theorem is false (circular Birkhoff use; explicit counterexample) and Part 21 swaps measures; Part 5 Thm 7.1 (residual half-frequency) is false. Problem 3: wrong input model, and its lemmas fail at n=1.
sources.relevance: Most elaborate 2026 claim; refuted.

sources.what_it_proves: Nothing about the prizes. It gives 200-step statistics and the cycle structure (lengths 1+2+5) of an 8-state shift map.
sources.rigor: Invalid. Its 'FSM' is not the cellular automaton, and every orbit of an 8-state map is eventually periodic. The balance claim assumes the conclusion. The 'dependency cone ⇒ Ω(n)' argument is refuted by Rule 150.

sources.what_it_proves: Per the abstract: linear degree growth and an Ω(n) decision-tree bound for f_n (the center bit as a function of all 2n+1 initial bits). This is plausibly true; my computation gives degree 2n−1 for Rule 30, n ≤ 6.
sources.rigor: Full text not accessed (SSRN human-verification page). The stated inferences to non-periodicity and to Ω(n) effort for the seed are invalid: Condrey's checkerboard initial condition has the same f_n but center ≡ 1.

sources.what_it_proves: Only that the standard bit-shift simulation (V<<1)^(V|(V>>1)) matches CellularAutomaton for 20 steps.
sources.rigor: No theorem is stated or proved.

sources.title: Condrey, 'Finite Configurations Cannot Generate a Constant Trace in Rule 30' (arXiv 2609.09431, Sept 2026)
sources.what_it_proves: (1) Classifies all configurations with center trace ≡ 0 (left half = prefix-OR of the right half, eventually alternating) and ≡ 1 (one universal checkerboard left half). (2) No column of any nonzero finite Rule 30 orbit is eventually constant. (3) Sharp maximum constant prefix of w+2 for support radius w. (4) Remark: for period 2 the horizon is at least w, so no bounded law exists. Explicitly not a prize claim.
sources.rigor: Rigorous. Short proofs; I verified Theorems 2–3 and the horizon table (w ≤ 7) numerically. Its Lean file is only a partial formalization.
sources.relevance: The strongest recent rigorous partial result on Problem 1 (period-1 case, all finite seeds). It matches and generalizes our Lean result and states that period 2 is next.

sources.title: Kopra, 'A natural class of cellular automata containing fractional multiplication automata, Rule 30, and others' (arXiv 2202.13809; published as 'Rapid left expansivity, a commonality between Wolfram's Rule 30 and powers of p/q', TCS 946 (2023) 113668)
sources.what_it_proves: Thm 3.5: for 'rapidly left expansive' rules (including Rule 30), no width-w block of columns is eventually periodic from any nonzero left-bounded configuration (width 2 for Rule 30, i.e. Jen's adjacent-column result). Thms 4.5 and 4.7: a recurrence and a limit-point result for such rules. Problem 4.8 is Prize Problem 1. Notes that Rule 90 is in this class but has an eventually periodic single-seed center column.
sources.rigor: Peer-reviewed, rigorous.
sources.relevance: Best published generalization of Jen; sets a barrier: rapid left expansivity alone cannot settle Problem 1.

sources.title: Jen, 'Global properties of cellular automata', J. Stat. Phys. 43 (1986) 219–242; Jen, 'Aperiodicity in one-dimensional cellular automata', Physica D 45 (1990) 3–18
sources.what_it_proves: A finite Rule 30 orbit has at most one eventually periodic column (1986, Thm 2b; 1990, Prop. 3). Gives conditions for eventually-one columns (1986, Thm 7a), which already exclude eventually-1 columns for finite Rule 30 configurations.
sources.rigor: Peer-reviewed, rigorous.
sources.relevance: The main classical result; already in our Lean (Rule30Jen.lean). Cited by Wolfram and listed in the prize bibliography.

sources.title: Nersissian, 'Diagonal Periods and Newton Supports of Rules 30, 86 and 135' (arXiv 2609.25077) and 'Diagonal Bases and Diagonal Periods of Elementary Cellular Automata' (arXiv 2609.25078), Sept 2026
sources.what_it_proves: Thm 8: diagonal R_{m-1} (our notation) is purely periodic with least period 2^{⌈log2(max S_m+1)⌉} ≥ ⌊m/2⌋+1, where S_m is its Newton support; record periods double infinitely often. Thm 7: max S_m ≤ F_{m+1}−1 (Fibonacci ceiling). Thm 13: the largest left-side (Rule 86) period up to depth m is at least ½·log2(m+2).
sources.rigor: Thm 8 is elementary and correct (checked by reading). Thm 13 not checked. States explicitly that it does not determine the center column.
sources.relevance: Partial results on diagonals, directly formalizable on top of Rule30Diagonals.lean. The author reports a prize-form submission (Jan 2026) with no public outcome.

sources.title: Wolfram, 'Announcing the Rule 30 Prizes' (Stephen Wolfram Writings, Oct 2019)
sources.what_it_proves: Official formal statements. P1: NotExists[{p,i}, ForAll[t, t>i, c[t+p]==c[t]]]. P2: DiscreteLimit[Total[c]/t] == 1/2. P3: no finite machine with lim sup effort/n < ∞. Also: non-periodic for the first 10^9 steps (by computation); Jen 1986; ring periods ≈ 2^{0.63n}; P3 affirmative ⇒ P1 affirmative; below-O(n²) effort called 'a nice partial result'.

sources.relevance: Defines the targets and the known status. Note the literal P3 formal statement (no O(n) machine) is stronger than the prose.

useful_theorems: Jen 1986/1990 (Kopra TCS 2023 generalization): for Rule 30 and any nonzero left-bounded configuration, no two adjacent columns are jointly eventually periodic; a finite orbit has at most one eventually periodic column. Already in Rule30Jen.lean.

Condrey 2026, zero-trace fiber (Thm 2). Notation: R_j = x_j and L_j = x_{−j} are the cells right and left of center, m is the position of the first 1 in R. If the center starts at 0 with right half R ≠ 0, the trace is identically 0 iff the left half is L_j=0 (j<m), L_m=1, L_j=j mod 2 (j>m). Prefix-OR form: L_{2k+1}=OR_{j≤2k+1} R_j, L_{2k}=R_{2k} ∧ ¬OR_{j≤2k−1} R_j. If R = 0, only the zero row works. Proof: one-step invariance of classes C_m plus left-permutive uniqueness (Lemma 1). Numerically verified.

Condrey 2026, all-one fiber (Thm 3): x_0=1 with x_{−j}=1 iff j is positive and even, and an arbitrary right half, gives center ≡ 1 under Rule 30. The left half is fixed by F. Barrier consequence: Rule 30 has initial conditions with constant center trace, so any proof of Problem 1 must use specific properties of the seed (e.g. finite support or left edge), not just the local rule, permutivity, or degree/decision-tree properties of the n-step map.

Condrey 2026 Cor. 4–5: no column of a nonzero finite Rule 30 orbit is eventually constant. Eventually-1 column c forces left neighbour l_t = 1⊕c_{t+1} = 0, then use the zero case. Sharp horizon (Thms 6–7, Cor. 8): a nonzero row supported in [−w,w] keeps its center constant for at most w+2 symbols; extremizer counts 2^w (w even) and 2^w−1 (w odd). Remark: the period-2 horizon H(2,w) ≥ w, so no bounded law exists.

Left-permutive trace bijection (Condrey Lemma 1; standard): for a fixed right half x_{≥0}, the map from left half to center trace is a homeomorphism onto traces starting with x_0, and (F^t x)_0 = x_{−t} ⊕ H_t(x_{−t+1..t}). Consequences: under uniform Bernoulli initial data the center trace is i.i.d. uniform, so Problems 1–2 hold for almost every random initial condition. The trace map is open, so eventually periodic traces come from a meagre set (true), and frequency-1/2 traces also come from a meagre set (my derivation; refutes Fradkin Part 5 Thm 7.1).

Nersissian 2026 Thm 8 (elementary, formalizable): right diagonal R_j (R j t = cell t (t−j)) is 0 for t < ⌈j/2⌉ and 1 at t = ⌈j/2⌉, because the two leftmost cells of the cone are 1 for t ≥ 1. Since R_j is purely periodic, its least period P_j > ⌈j/2⌉, so P_j ≥ 2^{⌈log2(⌈j/2⌉+1)⌉} and diagonal periods are unbounded; record periods double. Upper bound (Thm 7): the Newton support satisfies max S ≤ F_{j+2}−1, so P_j ≤ 2^{⌈log2 F_{j+2}⌉}.

Newton/Lucas fact used above: a 0/1 sequence periodic from 0 with period dividing 2^k equals Σ_{i∈S} C(n,i) mod 2 for a unique S ⊆ [0,2^k), and its least period is 2^{bitlength(max S)}. The first nonzero index equals min S.

Kopra 2023 Thm 4.5/4.7 (Rule 30, nonzero left-bounded x): the right-tail fraction frac(F^t x) equals frac(x) for only finitely many t, and the sequence (frac(F^t x))_t has infinitely many limit points. Kopra's Problem 4.8 is exactly Prize Problem 1.

Counterexample rules for vetting arguments: Rule 90 (left-permutive, rapidly left expansive): single-seed center 1,0,0,…. Rule 150: center ≡ 1 (central trinomial coefficients odd: T_{2m} ≡ T_{2m+1} ≡ T_m mod 2). Rule 22 = Rule30 AND Rule150: degree of the n-step center map is 2n+1 for n ≤ 6, yet center 1,1,0,0,…. Rule 30 on any ring: all columns eventually periodic (cycle periods ≈ 2^{0.63L} per Wolfram).

Computed (anf_degree.py): algebraic degree over GF(2) of Rule 30's n-step center map is 2,3,5,7,9,11 for n=1..6. Since decision-tree depth ≥ degree, query complexity is Θ(n) for arbitrary inputs. This is irrelevant to Problem 3, whose input is just n for the fixed seed.

Official problem facts (Wolfram 2019): an affirmative Problem 3 implies an affirmative Problem 1 (an eventually periodic sequence is computable cheaply from n). The literal formal Problem 3 is NotExists[m, … && MaxLimit[effort/n] < ∞], a superlinear requirement stronger than the prose 'at least O(n)'.

result.summary:
Bottom line: nothing in Jen's two papers, or in any later work that cites them, proves or comes close to proving that the rule 30 center column from a single seed is not eventually periodic. Kopra (2022) and Condrey (2026) both say explicitly that the problem is still open.

**What Jen proved.** In Jen's terms a column ("temporal sequence") is "periodic" if it is eventually periodic. Her Proposition 3 (Jen 1990, credited there to Jen 1986, which Condrey cites as Thm 2b) covers rules that are left-permutive with 001→1, or right-permutive with 100→1. For such rules, any finite initial condition produces at most one eventually periodic column. With 000→0 assumed, these are exactly the elementary rules 30, 86, 90, 150, 154 and 210.

The proof works in three steps:
- Columns lying between two periodic columns are themselves eventually periodic.
- Permutivity then spreads periodicity outward from two adjacent periodic columns; for rule 30 it spreads to the left.
- That contradicts the edge of the pattern, which moves one cell per step.

The result gives infinitely many aperiodic columns. It says nothing about which column could be the one exception. This is already formalized in `Rule30Jen.lean`.

**Two errors in the 1990 preprint text**, neither of which affects Proposition 3:
- The Lemma claims the inner columns have a period dividing lcm(p_i, p_j). That is false: rule 108 started from 101 has columns 0 and 2 constant while column 1 has period 2. The correct statement, eventual periodicity proved by pigeonhole, is what the Lean proof uses.
- Proposition 2's exceptional case for rule 90 leaves out the single seed, whose center column is 1,0,0,…

**Jen 1986 full text was not readable here.** The Springer copy is paywalled and blocks automated access, OSTI has no scan of the 1985 preprint LA-UR-85-1218, and zbMATH only has the abstract. Its theorem content is reconstructed from:
- the 1990 preprint, which credits the Lemma and Proposition 3 to the 1986 paper;
- Condrey's citations of Thm 2b and Thm 7a (Thm 7a's necessary condition already rules out an eventually-1 column for finite rule 30 initial conditions);
- Rowland's citation of Thm 4: every column of a one-sided rule is eventually periodic from an initial condition whose left tail is constant, which for rule 30 means every left diagonal is eventually periodic.

**Closest results to the single-column problem:**
1. **Jen:** no two columns are both eventually periodic.
2. **Kopra 2022 (Thm 3.5):** no pair of adjacent columns is eventually periodic, for any configuration that is zero to the left of some point, even with an infinite right half. The general framework has no width-1 version for rule 30, and I proved here that rule 30 is not "left expansive with width 1". The width-1 analogue does hold for fractional-multiplication automata (Kopra 2020, Prop 2.8).
3. **Wolfram's book (NKS p.1087), made rigorous here:** if column i is eventually periodic, then x_i ∨ x_{i+1} (equivalently, column i+1 read only at the times column i is 0) is not.
4. **Period 1 only:** our Lean result covers the single seed; Condrey 2026 Cor 5 covers every nonzero finite initial condition, using the OR "latch". Condrey shows the period-2 case already has no bounded analogue.

**Barrier.** Proved here and checked numerically: four of Jen's six rules have an eventually periodic single-seed center column — 90 gives 1,0,0,…; 150 gives all 1s; 210 = x⊕(¬y∧z) and its mirror 154 reproduce the rule 90 pattern exactly. Only 30 and its mirror 86 are open. So a proof cannot rest on one-sided permutivity, 001→1, nonlinearity and asymmetry alone; it has to use rule 30's OR.

**Two consequences for the brief's driven-halves plan:**
- Jen's argument shows that the left half driven by any eventually periodic, non-zero c never has an eventually periodic column −1. Left-driven runs can therefore never exclude a word, which matches the numerics.
- The criterion for excluding a word on the right side can be weakened: c = w^∞ is excluded as soon as column 1 is eventually periodic on the time steps where w is 0. Column 1 does not need to be periodic on every residue mod |w|.

Scratch files are in /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30prize/jen-lit/:
- `ocr1990/p-01..22.txt`: OCR of the Jen 1990 preprint; pages p-06, p-08, p-09, p-10 were checked against the scan images.
- `scripts/lemma_check.py`: rule 108 counterexample to the Lemma.
- `scripts/jen_class_columns.py` and `scripts/barrier_checks.py`: the barrier checks.
- `scripts/width1_not_expansive.py`: the width-1 construction, checked for K ≤ 40.

sources.title: E. Jen, 'Aperiodicity in one-dimensional cellular automata', Los Alamos preprint LA-UR-90-761 (CONF-8908218-1), scanned at UNT/OSTI; OCR checked against page images
sources.what_it_proves:
- Definitions: a column is 'periodic' when it is eventually periodic (period p, transience T); a finite initial condition is one with compact support; a rule is 'injective in component k' when it is permutive in that variable.
- Prop 1: every linear rule except rule 0 is injective in at least one component; rule 30 is injective in the (i−1) component but is not linear.
- Prop 2: rule 90 columns are aperiodic except for one 'trivial' symmetric case.
- Lemma (credited to Jen 1986): two periodic columns force every column between them to be periodic.
- Prop 3 (credited to Jen 1986): if R is injective in the (i+1) component with 100→1, or in the (i−1) component with 001→1, then any finite initial condition gives at most one periodic column. Jen states this holds for rules 30, 86, 90, 150, 154, 210.
- Props 4–5: rule 18, mapped exactly onto rule 90, has aperiodic columns except in a trivial case.
sources.rigor:
Short proofs. Prop 3's proof is essentially sound, given a correctly stated Lemma.
- The Lemma's claim that the inner period divides lcm(p_i, p_j) is false. Counterexample checked here: rule 108 from 101 has columns 0 and 2 constant and column 1 of period 2.
- Prop 2's exceptional case is too narrow: the single seed (center cell 1) gives the center column 1,0,0,…, which is eventually periodic.
- The preprint text says 'at most one aperiodic temporal sequence' and 'periodic temporal condition'; both are slips for the obvious meaning.
sources.relevance: Primary source for Jen's theorem, which is already formalized in Rule30Jen.lean. It leaves open which single column might be the exception, and that is exactly Prize Problem 1.

sources.title: E. Jen, 'Aperiodicity in one-dimensional cellular automata', Physica D 45 (1990) 3–18 (journal version)
sources.what_it_proves: Same results as the preprint. Kopra (2022) and Condrey (2026) both cite the at-most-one-periodic-column result as 'Prop. 3' of this version, so the numbering matches. The journal version has 18 references against the preprint's 12, so it is longer; for example, it presumably defines the 'Class A/B' rules the preprint mentions without defining.
sources.rigor: Not accessed: ScienceDirect blocks automated access. The extra material is unverified.
sources.relevance: Citation target only. The content was taken from the preprint.

sources.title: E. Jen, 'Global properties of cellular automata', J. Stat. Phys. 43 (1986) 219–242 (preprint LA-UR-85-1218)
sources.what_it_proves:
Abstract, verbatim from OSTI 5674011 / zbMATH 0638.68043: 'A class of cellular automata that generate infinitely many aperiodic temporal sequences is defined, as is the set of rules for which inverses exist. Necessary and sufficient conditions are derived characterizing the classes of nearest-neighbor rules for which arbitrary finite initial conditions (i) evolve to a homogeneous state; (ii) generate at least one constant temporal sequence.'

Theorems known only second-hand:
- Lemma and Prop 3 of Jen 1990 are credited to this paper; Condrey cites the result as Thm 2b.
- Thm 4 (per Rowland): columns of any one-sided [−d,0] rule are eventually periodic from an initial condition with a constant left tail.
- Thm 7a (per Condrey): necessary and sufficient conditions for an eventually-one column. Rule 30 (a0=0, a1=a4=1, a5=a6=a7=0) fails all four alternatives.
sources.rigor: Full text not accessed: Springer bot wall, no OSTI scan of the preprint, and the zbMATH review is just the abstract. Theorem wording is unverified.
sources.relevance: Original source of the 'at most one periodic column' theorem. Thm 4 underlies the diagonal results already in Lean.

sources.title: S. Wolfram, 'Random sequence generation by cellular automata', Adv. Appl. Math. 7 (1986) 123–169, §6
sources.what_it_proves: Verbatim: 'One can prove in fact that only one such vertical sequence (obtained from any initial state containing a finite number of nonzero sites) can possibly be periodic [22]. For if two sequences were both periodic, then it would follow that all sequences to their right must also be, which would lead to a contradiction at the edge of the pattern.' Here [22] is Jen, LA-UR-85-1218. For rule 30 the propagation actually runs to the left: Wolfram's eq. 3.3 solves for a_{i−1}. He also notes that diagonals at angles ±1 must become periodic, and that the center column showed no period up to length 2^19.
sources.rigor: Expository restatement of Jen's result.
sources.relevance: Earliest secondary statement of Jen's result; it pins down the 1985 preprint number.

sources.title: J. Kopra, 'A natural class of cellular automata containing fractional multiplication automata, Rule 30, and others', arXiv:2202.13809; journal version 'Rapid left expansivity, a commonality between Wolfram's Rule 30 and powers of p/q', TCS 946 (2023) 113668
sources.what_it_proves:
- Thm 3.5: if F is 'rapidly left expansive' with width w and x is a nonzero configuration that is zero left of some point, then no width-w block of adjacent columns is eventually periodic. 'Rapidly left expansive' means: w adjacent columns locally determine the column to their left, the leftmost nonzero cell moves left, and a speed inequality holds.
- Rule 30 qualifies with width 2.
- Lemma 3.2: periodicity of a width-w block passes one column to the left.
- Thms 4.5–4.7 concern the right halves frac(F^t x) of the configuration.
- Problem 4.8 (Problem 3.10 in the journal version) is the single-seed rule 30 center column, explicitly open.
- Kopra notes that rule 90, which belongs to the same class, has an eventually periodic single-seed column.
sources.rigor: Complete proofs; peer reviewed.
sources.relevance: High. Extends Jen to initial conditions that are zero on the left but arbitrary on the right, and to a wider class of rules. Identifies width 1 as the gap; this report proves rule 30 is not left expansive with width 1.

sources.title: J. Kopra, 'On the trace subshifts of fractional multiplication automata', arXiv:2005.05112; TCS 851 (2021) 92–110
sources.what_it_proves: Prop 2.8, verbatim: 'Let p > q. If x is a configuration that represents a positive real number (in particular, if x is a finite configuration different from 0^Z), then Tr_{Π_{p/q,pq}}(x) is not eventually periodic.' In words: a single column of the multiply-by-p/q automaton is never eventually periodic. Kopra adds: 'The same idea has been used for other cellular automata in [Jen 1990].'
sources.rigor: Complete proof.
sources.relevance: Single-column (width-1) analogue of Problem 1, solved because one column determines its left neighbour. Shows exactly which property rule 30 lacks.

sources.title: D. L. Condrey, 'Finite Configurations Cannot Generate a Constant Trace in Rule 30', arXiv:2609.09431 (Sept 2026)
sources.what_it_proves:
- Lemma 1: two configurations that agree at all coordinates i ≥ 0 and have the same center column are equal.
- Thm 2: for a right half with R0=0 whose first 1 is at m, the unique left half giving an all-zero center column is L_j=0 for j<m, L_m=1, L_j = j mod 2 for j>m.
- Thm 3: for R0=1, the unique left half giving an all-one center column has L_j=1 exactly for positive even j.
- Cor 4 and Cor 5: no column of a nonzero finite rule 30 orbit is eventually zero, or eventually constant.
- Thms 6–8: a configuration supported in [−w,w] keeps its center constant for at most w+2 steps (sharp).
- Cites Jen 1986 Thm 2b, Jen 1990 Prop 3 and Jen 1986 Thm 7a.
- States that period 2 has no bounded analogue (H(2,w) ≥ w) and that every non-constant period remains open.
sources.rigor: New preprint, not peer reviewed. The arguments are elementary and look complete. The bundled Lean file is a partial formalization by the author's own account.
sources.relevance: Period-1 exclusion for all finite initial conditions; this generalizes the Lean result for the single seed. Lemma 1 (center column plus right half determines left half) is a usable tool.

sources.title: E. S. Rowland, 'Local nested structure in rule 30', Complex Systems 16 (2006) 239–258
sources.what_it_proves:
- Lemma 2: for a 'right bijective' one-sided rule, if the d columns to the left are periodic, column m is periodic from the start (not just eventually), with period dividing l(k)·lcm. As a result, rule 30's right diagonals are periodic with power-of-2 periods.
- Thm 1: local nested structure.
- Prop 2: proves Wolfram's period-doubling rule for left diagonals, from any initial condition with a constant left tail.
- Cites Jen 1986 Thm 4: columns of [−d,0] rules from such initial conditions are eventually periodic, so each left diagonal of rule 30 is eventually periodic with a power-of-2 period.
sources.rigor: Peer reviewed, with proofs.
sources.relevance: Diagonal results, already in Rule30Diagonals.lean. Main source for what Jen 1986 Thm 4 says.

sources.title: J. Gravner, D. Griffeath, 'Robust periodic solutions and evolution from seeds in one-dimensional edge cellular automata', TCS 466 (2012)
sources.what_it_proves: Prop 3.3, verbatim: 'A left permutative edge CA has no periodic solutions, thus no RPS.' In the frame that moves with the left edge, this means no initial condition that is zero on the left makes all left diagonals periodic with a common period. Rule 30 (E1D0) is the example.
sources.rigor: Proof given.
sources.relevance: Low to medium: it concerns diagonals near the edge, not vertical columns.

sources.title: S. Wolfram, 'Announcing the Rule 30 Prizes' (2019)
sources.what_it_proves: States that 'Erica Jen showed in 1986 that no two columns can both become periodic' and that 'a single column plus scattered cells in another column can't both be periodic' (linking the NKS p.1087 note). Also: 'there's no known way to extend the argument to a single column—such as the center column'.
sources.rigor: Expository.
sources.relevance: Problem statement and status.

sources.title: S. Wolfram, NKS notes: 'Cryptographic properties of rule 30' (p.1087) and 'Rule 30' (p.871)
sources.what_it_proves:
- p.1087, verbatim: 'Given two complete adjacent columns page 601 shows how all columns any distance to the left can be found. It turns out that this can be done even if the right-hand one of the two adjacent columns is not complete. So for example whenever there is a black cell in the left column it is irrelevant what appears in the right column.' Also: all 2^t single columns of length t occur.
- p.871 (https://www.wolframscience.com/nks/notes-2-1--rule-30/), verbatim: 'Erica Jen showed in 1986 that no pair of columns can ever repeat, and the arguments on page 1087 suggest that neither can the center column together with occasional neighboring cells.'
sources.rigor: Informal.
sources.relevance: Source of the 'column plus scattered cells of its right neighbour' corollary, proved rigorously in the theorems list.

sources.title: L. Gray, 'A Mathematician Looks at Wolfram's New Kind of Science', Notices AMS 50(2) (2003)
sources.what_it_proves: Restates Jen: 'The best mathematical result that I know about Rule 30 is due to Erica Jen, who proved that with the initial state in Figure 1, the sequence of colors attained in any two adjacent cells is not periodic.'
sources.rigor: Expository. The quote comes from the Semantic Scholar citation context; the AMS PDF returned 403.
sources.relevance: Accurate but weaker than what Jen proved.

sources.title: Papers that misstate Jen's result: J. Holden (Bridges 2017); S. Best & X. Xu (ICCAD 2019); Y. Luo et al. (IEEE TCAS-I 2020)
sources.what_it_proves: Nothing. Holden: Wolfram's 1984 conjecture of aperiodic behavior 'was proved by Erica Jen in 1986'. Best–Xu and Luo et al.: 'According to the formal proof in [Jen 1990], except the regularity of the left edge, the colors ... of CA30 are unpredictable.'
sources.rigor: Overclaims or misattributions. Jen proved only that at most one column is periodic.
sources.relevance: Warning: these must not be cited as evidence.

sources.title: zbMATH Open records 0638.68043 (Jen 1986) and 0729.68057 (Jen 1990)
sources.what_it_proves: The 1986 review is just the abstract. The 1990 summary is unavailable because of licensing.
sources.rigor: Bibliographic.
