result.summary:
Short version: I did not prove Problem 1, and I did not exclude period 2 for every transient. I found no complexity, return-word or recurrence argument that forces aperiodicity. Every such statement turns out to be equivalent to Problem 1 or to one of its period-bounded cases. What I did get is a set of rigorous reductions and barriers, five Lean files that compile with no sorry, and a sharper picture of where the difficulty sits.

Lean files (all in /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30prize/complexity/lean/, compiled with `cd ruliology-lean && lake env lean FILE`, standard axioms only):
- **Rule30Realize.lean.** Fix any right half (positions ≥ 1) and any target sequence for column 0. Exactly one left half makes column 0 equal that target. So:
  - every eventually periodic column can be realized;
  - only left-finiteness can rule it out;
  - for every n, some configuration agrees with the single seed at all positions ≥ −n, matches the true center column up to time n, and is white forever after.
- **Rule30Barrier.lean.**
  - Jen's adjacent-column theorem holds for every rule `left xor g(center,right)` with g(0,0)=0 and g(0,1)=1.
  - Yet rules 90, 150 and 210 have eventually constant center columns. Rule 210 is nonlinear, not mirror-symmetric, and left- but not right-permutive, just like rule 30.
  - Diagonal periodicity also holds for these rules (proof in text).
  - So left-permutivity, the light cone, Jen's theorem and diagonal periodicity cannot decide Problem 1, not even period 1. The only rule-30-specific ingredient used so far is that OR is monotone.
- **Rule30LeftDriven.lean.** In the left half driven at its boundary by any eventually periodic column, starting from a left-finite nonzero state, column −1 is never eventually periodic (Jen inside the half-line). So the left half can never absorb a pattern; only the right half can.
- **Rule30Period2.lean.** A hypothetical eventual period 2 forces this shape:
  - column −1 is black at every even step;
  - s_k := column −1 at odd steps has no "00";
  - column 1 at odd steps is the complement of s;
  - columns −2 and −3 are fixed functions of s;
  - column −4 is white at every odd step.
- **Rule30Complexity.lean.** Morse–Hedlund counting with a kernel-checked sorted-window certificate (all 16359 windows of length 26 are distinct). Any eventual period P with transient T has T+P ≥ 16359. This complements the existing window (P ≤ 4096, T ≤ 8192).

Other rigorous results (text proofs):
- The Morse–Hedlund, right-special-factor, ω-limit-set and return-word reformulations.
- From the 10^7-bit data file, T+P ≥ 9,999,957. This is subsumed by the billion-bit window in the brief.
- Constraint A: when c(t)=1, the next center value is the negation of column −1. So an eventual pattern w forces the left-finite left half, driven by w^∞, to satisfy a periodic constraint involving no right-half cells.
- S0 refinement: if c is eventually periodic, column 1 restricted to the times where c=0 is not eventually periodic.
- Geometry of runs:
  - 1-runs of c are exactly alternating blocks of the row ending at the center;
  - 0-runs of c are exactly stretches where columns −1 and 1 agree.
- Period 1 generalizes: for every nonzero left-finite seed, no column is eventually constant.

Main conjecture (the Left-half Conjecture, LHC). For every periodic driver containing a 1, no left-finite left half satisfies constraint A forever.
- LHC implies Problem 1, and also the version for every left-finite seed (GP1).
- Evidence:
  - exhaustive searches over left-finite supports up to L=36 for w=10 and L≤14–20 for all primitive w of length ≤ 5: maximum survival is about L divided by the density of 1s in w, exactly the random-coin heuristic, with no structured survivors;
  - 700 random finite seeds × 81 columns showed no eventually periodic column.

Why period 2 is the real frontier. It cannot be excluded by any of the following:
- right-half absorption: the column-1 words realizable by any right half under driver (10)^∞ number 2,3,5,…,188,237 for n=1..15, ratio about 1.26, apparently positive entropy;
- forced cells: under the period-2 hypothesis nothing is forced to a fixed value beyond column −4;
- Jen's theorem.

So the left edge has to be carried to the center in a way that goes beyond Jen.

claims.statement: For f: N→{0,1} let p_f(n) be the number of distinct length-n factors. The following are equivalent: (i) f is eventually periodic; (ii) p_f(n) ≤ n for some n≥1; (iii) p_f is bounded; (iv) for some n no length-n factor u is right-special (u0 and u1 both factors); (v) the omega-limit subshift X_f (two-sided sequences all of whose factors occur infinitely often in f) is finite; (vi) some factor occurring infinitely often has an eventually constant sequence of return words. If f(t+P)=f(t) for all t≥T then p_f(n) ≤ T+P for all n, and with P minimal, |X_f| = P. Consequently: Problem 1 ⟺ p_c(n) ≥ n+1 for all n ⟺ c has right-special factors of every length ⟺ X_c infinite ⟺ no factor has eventually constant return words; and 'c has no eventual period ≤ Q for any transient' ⟺ |X_c| > Q. Return words to 0 (resp. 1) are unbounded iff c has arbitrarily long 1-runs (resp. 0-runs); unbounded return words imply Problem 1 but are strictly stronger.
claims.proof: (i)⇒p_f(n)≤T+P: for i≥T the factor f[i,i+n) equals f[i',i'+n) with i'=T+((i−T) mod P), so all factors start in [0,T+P). (ii)⇒(i) (Morse–Hedlund): if f is constant we are done; else p(1)=2. Every length-m factor extends to the right, so restriction F_{m+1}→F_m is onto and p is nondecreasing. If p(n)≤n, p cannot increase at every step from 1 to n (that would give p(n)≥n+1), so p(m+1)=p(m) for some m<n; then restriction is a bijection, each length-m factor has a unique right extension, so f(i+m) is a function of f[i,i+m); the window sequence follows a map on a finite set, hence is eventually periodic. (iii)⇔(i) similarly. (iv): if no length-n factor is right-special, f(i+n) is a function of f[i,i+n) and the same argument applies; conversely if f is eventually periodic with (T,P) and n≥T+P, any occurrence at i has i+n−P≥T and i+n−P≥i, so f(i+n)=f(i+n−P) is read off inside the window. (v): if f is eventually periodic, X_f is the finite orbit of the periodic tail, with |X_f| = minimal period. If X_f is finite with K points, all are periodic and the factors occurring infinitely often number ≤K for each length; only finitely many length-n factors occur finitely often, so beyond their last occurrence the tail has p(n)≤K<n for n>K, and Morse–Hedlund applies to the tail. (vi): with (T,P) minimal and u=f[T,T+P), any occurrence j≥T of u is at a phase whose length-P window equals the period word, so it is a rotation equal to itself, which forces j≡T (mod P) by minimality; occurrences beyond T are exactly T+kP and the return word is eventually constant. Conversely, eventually constant return word r gives f = prefix·r^∞. Runs: a 1-run of unbounded length means gaps between 0s are unbounded, so return words to 0 are unbounded, contradicting uniform recurrence of an eventually periodic tail (unless c is eventually 1, which is excluded).
claims.evidence: Standard; no new leverage: these restate Problem 1 or its period-bounded cases. Small-n complexity is automatically maximal from data (p_c(n)=2^n for n≤20 in the 10^7 prefix) and says nothing about tails.

claims.statement: For rule 30 on the full line: for every right half R ∈ {0,1}^{p≥1} and every sequence c: N→{0,1}, there is exactly one configuration x with x|_{p≥1}=R whose column 0 is c. Hence, for each fixed R, the map from (left half, x_0) to the column-0 sequence is a homeomorphism onto {0,1}^N. In particular every eventually periodic sequence, with any prescribed right half, is column 0 of some configuration (necessarily with a non-left-finite left half when the target is aperiodic-incompatible). Corollary (seed perturbation): for every n there is x agreeing with the single seed at every position ≥ −n whose column 0 equals the true center column at times ≤ n and is white at all times > n.
claims.proof:
Construction:
(1) Let rh be the right half driven at position 0 by c.
(2) Put y(t) = c(t+1) xor (c(t) or rh(t,1)).
(3) Build the left columns by left-permutivity: col_0=c, col_{-1}=y, col_{-m-2}(t) = col_{-m-1}(t+1) xor (col_{-m-1}(t) or col_{-m}(t)).
(4) Let x = (R on p≥1; col_{-m}(0) at −m).
By induction on t, the evolution of x equals rh on p≥1 and col_{-m}(t) on p=−m≤0. At column 0, rule(y(t),c(t),rh(t,1)) = c(t+1) by xor cancellation; at p=−m the identity rule(col_{-m-1}(t),col_{-m}(t),col_{-m+1}(t)) = col_{-m}(t+1) is again xor cancellation.
Uniqueness: two configurations with the same R and the same column 0 have equal right halves at all times (positions ≥1 see only column 0 and positions ≥1, induction on t). Then column −m−1 at time t equals col_{-m}(t+1) xor (col_{-m}(t) or col_{-m+1}(t)), giving equality column by column. Continuity both ways is immediate from the finite-dependence lemmas: the right half up to time t sees c only before t, and col_{-m}(t) sees c only up to m+t.
Seed corollary: the seed is the configuration built from (R_seed, center). Build x from (R_seed, c') with c' = center up to n and 0 afterwards. Then x_{-m} for m≤n depends only on c' up to m, which agrees with the center, so x agrees with the seed on [−n,∞).

claims.statement:
Let F_g be the CA new = left xor g(center,right) from a single black cell, with g(0,0)=0 and g(0,1)=1 (rule 30 is g=or).
(a) No two adjacent columns of F_g are both eventually periodic (Jen's adjacent theorem).
(b) Right diagonals R_j(t)=cell(t,t−j) are periodic from t=0 with power-of-2 periods, and left diagonals D_j(t)=cell(t,j−t) are eventually periodic.
(c) For g=right (rule 90) the center column is 1,0,0,…; for g=xor (rule 150) it is constantly 1; for g=(not center) and right (rule 210) it is 1,0,0,…. Rule 210 is nonlinear, not mirror-symmetric, and left- but not right-permutive, exactly like rule 30.
Therefore left-permutivity, the light cone and left edge, Jen's theorem, and diagonal periodicity together do not imply aperiodicity, not even the period-1 case. A proof of Problem 1 must use OR-specific structure; so far the only such ingredient in the library is OR-monotonicity in no_column_eventually_constant.
claims.proof:
(a) g(0,0)=0 gives cells left of −t white; g(0,1)=1 gives cell(t,−t)=1. Left-permutivity: cell(t,i−1) = cell(t+1,i) xor g(cell(t,i),cell(t,i+1)). If columns i and i+1 are periodic from a common T with a common P, so is every column to the left, by induction. A column q < −(T+P) is white at time −q−P ≥ T and black at time −q, contradicting periodicity.
(b) R_{j+2}(t+1) = R_{j+2}(t) xor g(R_{j+1}(t),R_j(t)), with R_{j+2}(0)=0, R_0≡1 (right edge, g(0,0)=0) and R_{-1}≡0. A running parity of a 2^e-periodic input is 2^{e+1}-periodic. Also D_{j+2}(t+1) = D_j(t) xor g(D_{j+1}(t),D_{j+2}(t)): a one-bit state driven by eventually periodic inputs is eventually periodic.
(c) Rules 90 and 150 are mirror-symmetric, so the seed pattern satisfies cell(t,−p)=cell(t,p) by induction. Then cell(t+1,0) = cell(t,−1) xor cell(t,1) = 0 for rule 90, and = cell(t,−1) xor cell(t,0) xor cell(t,1) = cell(t,0) = 1 for rule 150. For rule 210, induct jointly on 'cell210=cell90' and 'cell90(t,p)=1 ⇒ t+p even'. If t+1+p is odd, both neighbours have odd parity and are white, so the new cell is 0. If t+1+p is even, the center cell has odd parity and is white, so g = right and the rule acts as rule 90. Rule 90 and 150 are moreover bipermutive, hence positively expansive, yet still have eventually constant centers.

claims.statement: Global symbolic-dynamics theorems about a CA on the full shift cannot decide (a)periodicity of the single-seed center column. This covers Hedlund (surjective ⟺ balanced ⟺ pre-injective), permutivity, left/right-closing or open maps, positive expansivity and conjugacy to full shifts, mixing, and entropy. Two reasons: (1) for rule 30 itself, each right-half fiber of the column map is a homeomorphism onto {0,1}^N, so every sequence, periodic or not, is column 0 of uncountably many configurations; (2) bipermutive, positively expansive rules 90 and 150 (and rule 210, with rule 30's exact permutivity type) have eventually constant single-seed centers. What remains usable are orbit-specific facts: left-finiteness (the left edge), right-finiteness, and the exact single-seed content.
claims.proof: (1) is realization-uniqueness. (2) is barrier-jen-family (c), plus the standard fact that a bipermutive radius-1 CA is positively expansive. Any theorem whose hypotheses are global dynamical properties shared by rules 90 or 150, together with 'single seed / light cone / left edge', would also prove an aperiodic center for rule 90 or 150, which is false.

claims.statement: Let the left half p≤−1 evolve under rule 30 with position 0 fed by a column c (the 'driven left half'). If the initial left half is left-finite and not all white, and c is eventually periodic, then no column −m (m≥1) of the driven left half is eventually periodic. In particular the left half has no 'absorbing words'. The brief's observation that driven column −1 stays aperiodic for every word is a theorem: with seed driver 1·w^∞ the left half is nonzero from time 1.
claims.proof: Inside the half-line, left-permutivity cell(t,i−1) = cell(t+1,i) xor (cell(t,i) or cell(t,i+1)) holds for i≤−1, using columns i, i+1 ≤ 0, where column 0 = c. The leftmost black cell q of a left-finite state moves left one cell per step, with white cells beyond it. Adjacent case: if c and column −1 are both eventually periodic (common T, P), all columns ≤ −2 are too, and column q−(T+P)−1 is white at time T+1 but black at time T+P+1, a contradiction. General −m: the strip strictly between columns −m and 0 is a finite-state system driven by the two boundary columns. Pigeonhole makes column −m+1 eventually periodic, as in Rule30Jen.between_periodic, which reduces to the adjacent case.

claims.statement:
Suppose c(t+P)=c(t) for t≥T, with pattern w=c[T,T+P), S1={t≥T: c(t)=1} and S0={t≥T: c(t)=0}.
(a) Constraint A: for t∈S1, cell(t,−1) = not c(t+1). This is a condition on the left half alone, which for t≥T is the left half driven by w^∞ from its left-finite state at time T (support [−T,−1]).
(b) For t∈S0, cell(t,1) = c(t+1) xor cell(t,−1). The right half enters only through column 1 on S0.
(c) S0 refinement: column −1 is eventually periodic ⟺ column 1 restricted to S0 is eventually periodic. By Jen neither is, so to exclude w by absorption it suffices that column 1 at the phases where w=0 becomes periodic.
(d) By realization, A plus any right half is always satisfiable by a non-left-finite left half. So any contradiction must use left-finiteness, and must use it beyond Jen when the right half does not absorb.
(e) c is eventually w-periodic from T ⟺ the actual left half at time T equals the unique left half determined (as in realization-uniqueness) by the actual right half at time T and the target w^∞.
claims.proof: (a),(b): the rule at column 0 reads c(t+1) = cell(t,−1) xor (c(t) or cell(t,1)); for c(t)=1 the right term is 1, and for c(t)=0 it is cell(t,1). Cells at p≤−1 at time t+1 depend only on p≤0 at time t, so the left half is the half-line driven by c. (c): with m(t)=cell(t,1)·[c(t)=0], column −1 equals not c(t+1) on S1 and c(t+1) xor m(t) on S0, so it is eventually periodic iff m is. Jen (columns −1 and 0) excludes this. (d),(e): realization-uniqueness applied from time T.

claims.proof: Each item is the local rule at one cell. Even t: c(t+1)=0 = cell(t,−1) xor 1. Odd t: c(t+1)=1 = cell(t,−1) xor cell(t,1). Column −1 at t+1: cell(t,−2) xor (cell(t,−1) or c(t)), giving −2 at both phases. Column −2 at t+1 = not cell(t,−3), since (cell(t,−2) or cell(t,−1))=1 at both phases. Golden mean: s_k=0 ⇒ cell(T+2k+1,1)=1 ⇒ cell(T+2k+2,1)=1 ⇒ cell(T+2k+3,1)=0 = not s_{k+1}. Column −4: s_{k+1} = cell(T+2k+1,−4) xor (s_{k+1} or not s_k), and golden mean makes the OR 1 whenever s_{k+1}=0. Normalization: c(t+2)=c(t) for t≥T0 and c not eventually constant force c(T0)≠c(T0+1).

claims.statement:
For any column i of any rule-30 evolution:
- column i is 1 on [t,t+k) ⟺ the row at time t is alternating on [i−k+1, i] and black at i (…0101 then 1 at i);
- column i is 0 on [t,t+k) ⟺ cell(t,i)=0 and cell(s,i−1)=cell(s,i+1) for s∈[t,t+k−1).
So 'c has arbitrarily long 1-runs' (unbounded return words to 0) ⟺ rows contain arbitrarily long alternating blocks ending black at the center; and 'arbitrarily long 0-runs' ⟺ columns −1 and 1 agree on arbitrarily long stretches starting at a white center cell.
claims.proof: If cell(s,i)=1 then cell(s+1,i) = not cell(s,i−1), so a 1-run of length k is exactly cell(s,i−1)=0 for s∈[t,t+k−1). By left-permutivity this forces the triangle cell(s,i−m)=(m+1) mod 2 for s∈[t,t+k−1−m], in particular the alternating block in row t. Conversely, an alternating block ending black at i stays inside its shrinking triangle: each interior cell has a black cell among its center and right neighbours, so the new value is not(left) = itself, and column i stays 1. If cell(s,i)=0 then cell(s+1,i) = cell(s,i−1) xor cell(s,i+1).

claims.statement: For every left-finite, not all white configuration x (all positions ≥ some q white to the left), (a) no two columns of the rule-30 orbit are both eventually periodic, and (b) no column is eventually constant. So the proved period-1 case and Jen's theorem hold for all left-finite seeds, not only the single seed.
claims.proof: (a) Jen's proof uses only left-permutivity, the strip pigeonhole, and the left edge: the leftmost black cell q−t, with everything further left white. Every such x has this edge. (b) An eventually black column i forces column i−1 eventually white, since rule(l,1,r) = not l. An eventually white column i makes column i+1 nondecreasing, since rule(0,b,r) = b or r, hence eventually constant. Either way two adjacent columns are eventually periodic, contradicting (a).

LHC(w) for all such w implies GP1 and hence Problem 1. The right half and right-finiteness are not needed: eventually white is already excluded by GP1-period1. Equivalently, via the bijection x ↔ column −1 (fixed driver), the countable set of left-finite states never meets the Cantor set {x : col_{-1} = not c(·+1) on S1} ≅ {0,1}^{S0}.
claims.proof: Not proved. Proved parts: the reduction LHC ⇒ GP1 ⇒ Problem 1 (constraint-A-reduction (a) plus GP1-period1) and the case w=1. For w=1, A forces column −1 to be constantly white, and left-permutivity then forces the entire left half to be the alternating pattern …0101 (column −m = (m+1) mod 2), which is not left-finite. For other w, forcing dies out after about 3|w| columns, and A is satisfiable without left-finiteness (realization), so a proof must transport left-edge information to the boundary.

claims.statement: Period 2 cannot be excluded by right-half absorption, even allowing arbitrary (non-finite) right halves. The set of words z_k = cell(T+2k+1,1), k<n, realizable by some right half under driver (10)^∞ has sizes 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 17, 25, 36, 49, 65, 88, 115, 148, 188, 237 for n=1..15. Together with period2-skeleton and the absence of further forced cells, any proof of the period-2 case must use left-finiteness (or right-finiteness) beyond Jen.

result.failed_approaches:
1. Complexity, return words and recurrence. Every formulation is equivalent to Problem 1 or one of its period-bounded cases (see MH-reformulations). Data only gives window-type bounds such as T+P ≥ 16359 (Lean) and T+P ≥ 9,999,957 (from the 10^7-bit file); both are subsumed by or complement the existing windows. Proving unbounded return words is strictly harder: it needs arbitrarily long alternating blocks at the center, or long agreement of columns −1 and 1.

2. Global symbolic-dynamics theorems (Hedlund, closing maps, permutive, expansive, entropy). They do not apply to a single orbit. The column map's fibers over right halves are homeomorphisms onto {0,1}^N, and the rule-90/150/210 barrier shows that every structural property used so far is shared with rules whose center column is eventually constant.

3. Partial-periodicity propagation (a Jen-style rigidity cascade). Under each hypothesis w (10, 110, 1110, 11110, 111110), forced cells exist only near the center: for w=10 nothing is forced beyond column −4. So the left edge is never reached. Adding right-half realizability constraints did not help.

4. Right-half absorption for period 2. The realizable column-1 language for driver 10 grows exponentially (ratio about 1.26), so column 1 is not forced to be periodic. The S0 refinement (only phases where w=0 matter) did not turn any non-absorbing word of length ≤5 into an absorbing one.

5. Information or counting arguments via the bijection between the left half and column −1. They reproduce exactly the random heuristic (survival about L/d) but cannot be made rigorous without mixing properties of specific orbits.

6. Diagonal and 2-adic structure: right diagonals with periods 2^{e_j}, the parity identity, diagonal copies of the left half deep in the right half. All of it holds for rule 210 too, so it cannot force aperiodicity alone.

7. Kolmogorov complexity: c is computable, so this gives nothing.
result.most_promising_next_step:
Make period 2 the explicit frontier and attack it from the left, as the single-word conjecture LHC(10).

The question: driven by (10)^∞ from any left-finite state, can the left half keep column −1 black at every even step forever (with s golden-mean, from the right)? The results here show that right absorption, local forcing and Jen cannot settle this. A proof has to carry the left edge's information to the center. Two features help:
- the bijection between left-half states and column −1 turns the driven dynamics into a shift;
- the left edge always starts the same way: D0=D1=1, D2=0, D3 alternating, D4 eventually 1, …

Concrete first targets:
1. Prove LHC(1^{P−1}0). Here A forces long alternating triangles at the center, which a speed-1 signal from the edge must keep breaking.
2. Prove a quantitative LHC(10) for left halves whose left part already has the seed's settled diagonal structure.

In parallel, the absorb team can:
- use the S0 refinement (only column 1 at phases where w=0 needs to become periodic);
- use Rule30LeftDriven.not_both_periodic plus Rule30Realize as Lean glue: absorption of column 1 at the phases where w=0 excludes w for every left-finite configuration.

result.angle: diagonal structure (right diagonals R_j(t)=cell(t,t-j) with least period 2^{e_j}; left diagonals; c(t)=R_t(t)=D_t(t))
result.summary:
I found no obstruction to eventual periodicity of c, nor to any special family of periods (powers of 2, odd), from the diagonal structures. I did prove a complete structure theory for the right-diagonal period exponents e_j, and the Lean kernel checks it. File: /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30prize/diagonal/lean/RightPeriods.lean (591 lines, namespace Ruliology.CellularAutomata.Rule30RightPeriods). It imports Rule30Diagonals and Rule30Window and compiles in about 2 s with `cd ruliology-lean && lake env lean <file>`. Every main theorem depends only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound; there is no sorry and no native_decide.

Proven:
(1) Monotonicity (if R_{j+1} has period H, with H=1 or H even, so does every R_i for i<=j) and a shift formula. Together they give e_{j+1} = e_j + R_{j+1}(2^{e_j}), so each step is 0 or 1. The period doubles exactly when the cell at time 2^{e_j} on the next diagonal is black, and then the diagonal is complemented by half its period.
(2) e_n <= k exactly when row 2^k has n white cells just left of its right edge. Every row N reads 1 0^{J} 1 leftwards from its edge, with J = J_{nu2(N)} and J_k = max{j : e_j <= k}. Row 2^k-1 ends with 1^{J_k+1} 0.
(3) Restart: cell(N+s,N+q) = cell(s,q) whenever 0 <= s-q <= J_{nu2(N)}. So column 2^k u repeats c(0..J_k), and columns depend 2-adically continuously on their position.
(4) If c(t)=1 then 2^{e_t} > t.
(5) The period never doubles three times in a row.
(6) Bounds: j < 2^{e_j+1} and e_j <= floor((2j+1)/3).
(7) The guess e_j >= floor(j/2) is false: e_14 <= 6 and e_23 <= 8, both kernel-checked.
(8) Proved on paper only: a right-half parity identity, by which c(t) is fixed by the right half driven by c(0..t-1) through R_t(2^{e_t}) = 0. Also on paper: the right-edge window dynamics is conjugate to the 2-adic odometer, and the pre-history rows are 1^inf and (100)^inf.

Computation: an independent 128-bit window orbit gives J_E for E <= 37, which extends e_j to j=85 (e_85=37, e_j/j about 0.435). The zero-gap law matches a direct simulation of every row t <= 70000.

Why there is no obstruction: c(t) lies in the first period of R_t (proved whenever c(t)=1) and in the transient of D_t. So diagonal periodicity relates c(t) only to cells exponentially far away. The restart copies of c have length J_E, about 2.3E, which is logarithmic in their position — far too short for a pigeonhole or finite-Jen argument. Even the period-1 case is not recovered from these facts.

Scratch code and data are in /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30prize/diagonal/ (rdiag.c, window.c, gaps.c, stats.c, seedsearch.c, fakeright.c, prehistory.py, e_j_data.txt).

claims.statement: Let R_j(t)=cell(t,t-j) and let e_j be the least k such that R_j has period 2^k. (a) Monotonicity: for j>=2 and H=1 or H even, if R_{j+1} has period H then every R_i with i<=j has period H. For j=0,1 the same holds when H=2^k. Hence e_0<=e_1<=e_2<=... (b) Shift formula: if R_j has period 2^k then R_{j+1}(t+2^k) = R_{j+1}(t) xor R_{j+1}(2^k) for all t. (c) Hence for all j>=0, e_{j+1} = e_j + R_{j+1}(2^{e_j}), which is e_j or e_j+1. When the period doubles, R_{j+1}(t+2^{e_j}) = not R_{j+1}(t), so exactly half of each period is black. (d) For j>=3 the least period of the input g_j = R_{j-1} or R_{j-2} is exactly 2^{e_{j-1}}. So S_j := e_j - e_{j-1} is the parity of g_j over its least period, which is the brief's empirical rule, now proved.
claims.proof:
Notation: c(t)=cell(t,0). Per(j,p) means R_j(t+p)=R_j(t) for all t.

Known facts (Rule30Diagonals): R_0=1; R_1(0)=0 and R_1(t+1)=not R_1(t); R_{j+2}(t+1) = R_{j+2}(t) xor (R_{j+1}(t) or R_j(t)); Per(j,2^j). So e_j exists. Per(j,2^k) holds iff k>=e_j: if k>=e_j then 2^k is a multiple of 2^{e_j}; the converse is the minimality of e_j.

(F1) R_j(t)=0 if 2t<j, since position t-j < -t lies outside the light cone.
(F2) R_j(ceil(j/2))=1 for j>=1. For j=2s this is the left edge cell(s,-s)=1. For j=2s+1 it is cell(s+1,-s) = D_1(s+1) = 1.
(F3) R_2=R_1=(t mod 2): both start at 0 and flip every step, because R_2(t+1) = R_2(t) xor (R_1(t) or 1).
(L) If x(t+1)=x(t) xor g(t) and g has period L, then x(t+L) xor x(t) is constant (induction on t), so x(t+L) = x(t) xor x(L) xor x(0).

(a) Let j>=2, H=1 or H even, and Per(j+1,H). Write Z(a,M) for: R_a(H+t)=R_{a+1}(H+t)=0 for all t<M.
Step 1. For 2t+2<=j we have R_{j+1}(H+t)=R_{j+1}(t)=0 and R_{j+1}(H+t+1)=R_{j+1}(t+1)=0 by F1. The recurrence of R_{j+1} at s=H+t then forces (R_j or R_{j-1})(H+t)=0. Hence Z(j-1, floor(j/2)).
Step 2 (descent). Z(a+2,M+1) implies Z(a,M). For t<M, in R_{a+3}(s+1) = R_{a+3}(s) xor (R_{a+2}(s) or R_{a+1}(s)) at s=H+t, three of the four terms vanish, so R_{a+1}(H+t)=0. Then R_{a+2}(s+1) = R_{a+2}(s) xor (R_{a+1}(s) or R_a(s)) gives R_a(H+t)=0.
Step 3. Strong induction on i<=j.
- i=0: R_0 is constant.
- i=1: if H is even, t mod 2 has period H. If H=1, then R_{j+1} is constant, equal to R_{j+1}(0)=0, which contradicts F2.
- i=2: R_2=R_1.
- i=m+3<=j: by induction R_{m+2} and R_{m+1} have period H. By (L), R_{m+3}(t+H) = R_{m+3}(t) xor R_{m+3}(H), using R_{m+3}(0)=0. If R_{m+3}(H)=0 we are done. Otherwise let s=floor((j-m-3)/2) and a=j-1-2s. Then a is m+2 or m+3, a+2s=j-1, and 1+s<=floor(j/2). So Z(j-1,floor(j/2)) contains Z(a+2s,1+s), and s descents give Z(a,1). Then R_{m+3}(H)=0, a contradiction.
For j=0,1: R_0 is constant and R_1=R_2. Taking H=2^k gives e_i<=e_{j+1} for i<=j.

(b) For j=0, check directly with R_1=t mod 2. For j>=1: by (a), R_{j-1} also has period 2^k, so the input (R_j or R_{j-1}) of R_{j+1} has period 2^k. Apply (L) with R_{j+1}(0)=0.

(c) Take k=e_j. By (b), Per(j+1,2^{e_j+1}) always holds, and Per(j+1,2^{e_j}) holds iff R_{j+1}(2^{e_j})=0. Together with e_{j+1}>=e_j from (a), this is the formula. If R_{j+1}(2^{e_j})=1, then the shift complements R_{j+1}, so of the cells at t and t+2^{e_j} exactly one is black.

(d) In (a), Per(j+1,H) is used only through g_{j+1}(H+t)=g_{j+1}(t)=0 in Step 1, and for H=1 through g_{j+1} being identically g_{j+1}(0)=0, which forces R_{j+1}=0. So (a) also holds under the hypothesis that g_{j+1} has period H. For j>=2, g_{j+1} has period 2^{e_j}, so its least period is a power of 2 dividing 2^{e_j}. If that least period were smaller, g_{j+1} would have period H=2^{e_j-1}. Note e_j>=1 because R_j is non-constant by F1 and F2. Then all R_i with i<=j would have period H, contradicting the definition of e_j.

claims.statement: (a) R_n has period 2^k iff cell(2^k, 2^k-i)=0 for all 1<=i<=n. So e_n is the least k such that row 2^k has at least n white cells immediately left of its right edge. (b) Let J_k = max{j : e_j <= k}, which is finite with J_k>=k. For every N>=1, reading leftwards from the right edge of row N gives exactly J_{nu2(N)} white cells and then a black one, where nu2 is the 2-adic valuation. Explicitly, for N=2^k u with u odd: cell(N,N-i)=0 for 1<=i<=J_k and cell(N,N-J_k-1)=1. (c) If R_j has period 2^k then R_j(2^k-1)=1. Row 2^k-1 ends, leftwards from its edge, with exactly J_k+1 black cells and then a white one. (d) J_k <= 2^{k+1}-2. Values: J_0..J_37 = 0 2 3 5 6 8 14 15 23 24 26 28 33 35 36 38 40 42 47 48 50 53 54 57 59 62 63 65 68 69 71 73 76 78 79 81 83 85.
claims.proof:
(a) Forward: by mono_step_doubling(a), each R_i with i<=n has period 2^k, so R_i(2^k)=R_i(0)=0 (F1, i>=1). Backward, by induction on n: Per(0,2^k) is trivial, and if Per(n,2^k) and R_{n+1}(2^k)=0 then Per(n+1,2^k) by the shift formula. Note R_i(2^k)=cell(2^k,2^k-i).

(b) J_k is finite because e_j tends to infinity (bounds claim). J_k>=k because e_j<=j. For 1<=i<=J_k, R_i has period 2^k, so R_i(N)=R_i(0)=0. Put J=J_k. Then R_J has period 2^k and R_{J+1} does not. By mono_step_doubling(c), R_{J+1}(t+2^k) = not R_{J+1}(t), hence R_{J+1}(2^k u) = u mod 2 = 1.

(c) Induction on j.
- j=0: R_0=1.
- j=1: R_1 is not 1-periodic, so k>=1, and 2^k-1 is odd.
- j+2: R_{j+2}(2^k) = R_{j+2}(0) = 0, and also R_{j+2}(2^k) = R_{j+2}(2^k-1) xor (R_{j+1}(2^k-1) or R_j(2^k-1)). By induction R_{j+1}(2^k-1)=1, since R_{j+1} has period 2^k by monotonicity. So R_{j+2}(2^k-1)=1.
The white cell: R_{J+1} has period 2^{k+1}, so R_{J+1}(2^{k+1}-1)=1, and by the antiperiod R_{J+1}(2^k-1)=0.

(d) cell(2^k, -2^k+1) = D_1(2^k) = 1 lies at distance 2^{k+1}-1 from the right edge.

claims.statement: (a) Restart. If R_s has period 2^k, then cell(p+2^k u+s, p+2^k u) = cell(p+s, p) for all p,u>=0; in particular cell(2^k u+s, 2^k u) = c(s). More generally, cell(N+s, N+q) = cell(s,q) whenever 0 <= s-q <= J_{nu2(N)}: the initial triangle restarts at every right-edge cell (N,N). Column 2^k u repeats c(0),...,c(J_k), and for u odd, cell(2^k u+J_k+1, 2^k u) = not c(J_k+1). (b) If c(t)=1 then 2^{e_t} > t, so a black center cell lies in the first period of its right diagonal. (c) If 2^{e_t} <= t for some t>=1, then c=0 on [2^{e_t}, J_{e_t}], an interval containing [2^{e_t}, t].
claims.proof:
(a) If 2^k divides N and R_s has period 2^k, then cell(p+N+s, p+N) = R_s(p+N+s) = R_s(p+s) = cell(p+s, p). The general form uses j=s-q<=J_{nu2(N)}, so e_j<=nu2(N) and R_j(N+s)=R_j(s). The flip comes from the antiperiod: R_{J+1}(2^k u+J+1) = R_{J+1}(J+1) xor (u mod 2).

(b) Suppose 2^{e_t}<=t and let r = t mod 2^{e_t}. Then r<2^{e_t} and r<=t-2^{e_t}, so 2r<t. Hence c(t)=R_t(t)=R_t(r)=0 by periodicity and F1.

(c) Let E=e_t and N=2^E. Then t<=J_E. Every t' in [N,J_E] has e_{t'}<=E, so 2^{e_{t'}} <= N <= t', and c(t')=0 by (b).

claims.statement: For j>=1: 2^{e_j+1} > j; more sharply j <= 2^{e_j+1}-2. So e_j >= ceil(log2(j+2))-1, which tends to infinity. For j>=2: e_j <= floor((2j+1)/3). Both are tight for small j: e_4=3 and e_7=5 meet the upper bound.
claims.proof:
Lower bound: suppose 2^{k+1}<=j and R_j had period 2^k. Take s=ceil(j/2)>=2^k. Then R_j(s)=1 by F2, but R_j(s-2^k)=0 by F1, because 2(s-2^k) <= j+1-2^{k+1} < j. Contradiction. The sharper form follows from j <= J_{e_j} and rows_at_powers_of_two(d).

Upper bound: for j>=1, Per(j,2^k) implies Per(j+3,2^{k+2}). Proof by cases. If Per(j+1,2^k), apply the step bound twice. Else if Per(j+2,2^{k+1}), apply it once. Else no_three_doublings applies. With e_2=1, e_3=2, e_4=3 (from F3 and the step bound), induction gives e_j <= floor((2j+1)/3), since floor((2(j-3)+1)/3) + 2 = floor((2j+1)/3).
claims.lean_plan: Lean theorems not_per_small, per_three and per_upper. The sharper j<=2^{e_j+1}-2 is text-only.

claims.statement: Let S_j = e_j - e_{j-1}, which is 0 or 1. For j>=2: (a) if S_j=1, then R_j has exactly 2^{e_j-1} black cells per period; (b) if S_j=1, then S_{j+1} is congruent mod 2 to #{s<2^{e_{j-1}} : R_{j-1}(s)=1}, the black-cell parity of R_{j-1} over one period; (c) hence S_j=S_{j+1}=1 implies S_{j+2}=0, so the period never doubles three times in a row.
claims.proof:
Let H=2^{e_{j-1}}; H is even because e_{j-1}>=1 for j>=2.

(a) R_j(t+H) = not R_j(t), so each period [0,2H) contains exactly H black cells.

(b) S_{j+1} = R_{j+1}(2^{e_j}) = R_{j+1}(2H), which is the parity of the sum over s<2H of (R_j or R_{j-1})(s), using (L) and R_{j+1}(0)=0. Pair s with s+H for s<H. R_j flips, while R_{j-1} (period H) does not, and (a or b)+(not a or b) is 2 if b=1 and 1 if b=0. So S_{j+1} is congruent to #{s<H : R_{j-1}(s)=0}, which is congruent to #{s<H : R_{j-1}(s)=1} because H is even.

(c) Apply (b) at j+1: S_{j+2} is congruent to #{s<2^{e_j} : R_j(s)=1}. By (a) this count equals 2^{e_j-1}, which is even because e_j=e_{j-1}+1>=2. So S_{j+2}=0.
claims.lean_plan: Lean theorem no_three: for j>=1, Per j (2^E), not Per (j+1) (2^E) and not Per (j+2) (2^(E+1)) together imply Per (j+3) (2^(E+2)). The proof avoids counting. With x=R_{j+3}, H=2^E, put u(t)=x(t+2H) xor x(t), which accumulates not R_{j+1}, and v(t)=u(t+H) xor u(t), which flips every step. Then x(4H) = u(0) xor u(2H) = v(0) xor v(H) = 0 because H is even. Part (b) in general form is text-only.

claims.statement: For t>=1 and any K>=t that is a multiple of 2^{e_t}: c(t) = parity of #{s in [t,K) : cell(s,s-t+1) or cell(s,s-t+2)}. Every cell counted lies in columns >=1. Also, if 2^{e_{t-1}}>=t, then S_t = c(t) xor parity of #{s in [t, 2^{e_{t-1}}) : same condition}. Consequently c is determined recursively by the right half alone. R_{t-1} and R_{t-2} on [t, infinity), and also e_t, depend only on the right half driven by c(0..t-1), and c(t) is the unique bit making R_t(2^{e_t}) = 0.
claims.proof: For t>=1, R_t(s+1) = R_t(s) xor g_t(s), where g_t(s) = cell(s,s-t+1) or cell(s,s-t+2). For t=1 this is cell(s,s) or cell(s,s+1), which is 1. So R_t(K) = R_t(t) xor (parity of g_t over [t,K)). Here R_t(K)=R_t(0)=0 by periodicity and F1, and R_t(t)=c(t). The S_t formula is the same with K=2^{e_{t-1}}, using S_t = R_t(2^{e_{t-1}}). The least period of R_t equals that of its tail on [t, infinity). That tail is c(t) xor the running sum of g_t, and complementing does not change periods, so e_t depends only on g_t on [t, infinity). That in turn depends only on the right half driven by c(0..t-1).

claims.statement: Phi(tau)_i = R_i(tau mod 2^{e_i}) defines a homeomorphism Phi from the 2-adic integers Z_2 onto the orbit closure X of the right-edge window W(t)=(R_i(t))_i. It conjugates tau -> tau+1 to F(y)_i = y_i xor (y_{i-1} or y_{i-2}), where y_{-1}=y_{-2}=0. Its canonical pre-history: Phi(-1) is all ones and Phi(-2) = (100)^inf. Concretely, for k>=1, row 2^k-2 is black at distance i<=J_k from its right edge iff i is divisible by 3.
claims.proof:
Phi is well defined because R_i is 2^{e_i}-periodic, and it is continuous. It is equivariant on the natural numbers, hence on all of Z_2 by density. Injectivity: the window (R_0..R_i)(t) is an orbit of the bijection y_m <- y_m xor (y_{m-1} or y_{m-2}) on {0,1}^{i+1}, a lower-triangular map. Its least period is 2^{max of e_m for m<=i} = 2^{e_i}, so windows at a and b agree iff a = b mod 2^{e_i}. Since e_i tends to infinity, distinct tau are separated. The image is the orbit closure by compactness.
Phi(-1): R_i(2^{e_i}-1)=1 by rows_at_powers_of_two(c).
Phi(-2): from R_i(2^k-1)=1 and the recurrence, R_i(2^k-2) = not (R_{i-1}(2^k-2) or R_{i-2}(2^k-2)), with R_0=1 and R_{-1}=0. This gives 1,0,0,1,0,0,...

claims.statement:
Experiments relevant to an obstruction:
(i) For finite seeds of width <=16 (all 2^14 seeds of width 16, plus all smaller widths), no column within +-100 of the seed is P-periodic (P<=256) on t in [3000,6000]. The diagonal facts hold for every finite seed, so this agrees with a seed-independent version of Problem 1 but gives no lever.
(ii) For the right half driven by fake centers (true prefix up to T=12, then w^inf, with w in {0,1,01,10,001,011,0001,0111,0110}), the tail periods of the diagonals keep growing at about 0.4-0.5 doublings per diagonal. Periodic driving causes no collapse of the periods. The light-cone consistency of the periodic backward extension fails already at the first diagonal where the fake departs from the true c, which is automatic and gives no T-independent exclusion.
claims.proof: Experimental only (seedsearch.c, fakeright.c). For (ii) the failure is automatic: at the first deviation j0, the fake diagonal is the complement of the true one, so its extension is 1 at t=0.

result.failed_approaches:
1. Transporting c along its right diagonal. The relation c(t)=cell(t+k2^{e_t}, k2^{e_t}) only ties c(t) to cells exponentially later in far columns. Because c(t)=1 forces 2^{e_t}>t (proved), diagonal periodicity never relates two center values.

2. Restart copies plus Jen. Column 2^E u copies c[0..J_E], with J_E about 2.3E. A finite-window Jen argument needs two adjacent columns that are P-periodic on [T,T+L] with L at least T+2P+q, where q is the column position. Here only one column is periodic, and its window has length O(log of its position), so the argument fails by an exponential margin.

3. Left diagonals. c(t)=D_t(t) lies in the transient (T_t is about 1.34t). If the D_m were periodic from time m with a common period pi, column -pi would be a delayed copy of c and Jen would apply. That is false in reality, and the brief's experiments show periodic drivers do not settle the left half near the center.

4. Right-half self-consistency. The rule R_t(2^{e_t})=0 characterizes c exactly using the right half alone. But fakes are detected only at their first deviation, and periodic drivers leave the tail periods growing, so periodic driving has no diagonal signature.

5. Lower bounds on e_j beyond the logarithm. This is equivalent to non-sparsity of the right ends of rows 2^E. The scenario J_E>=2^E only forces c=0 on [2^E, J_E], which is not contradictory since c(2^E)=0 occurs.

6. More forced patterns in S. The parity argument closes only for consecutive doublings; otherwise product terms appear. In 85 bits of S, no length-4 word avoiding 111 is missing.

7. Even the period-1 case of Problem 1 is not derivable from the diagonal-period structure alone. The existing proof uses column arguments and Jen. Diagonal facts are essentially orthogonal to the values of the center column.

It is kernel-checked and has no sorry: monotonicity, the step bound and doubling law, zero gaps of rows 2^k u, ones-run at rows 2^k-1, restart and column continuity, black centers lying in the first period, no three consecutive doublings, the bounds, and the e_14/e_23 counterexamples.

The one lever this angle offers to other angles is the right-half reformulation (right_half_parity_identity): c(t) is the unique bit with R_t(2^{e_t})=0, computed from the right half driven by c(0..t-1). The driven-halves / absorbing-word program could use it as an exact consistency test in place of the left half.

Within the angle, the next nontrivial structural target is conj_first_period: row 2^E always has a black cell in [0,2^E). After that comes conj_linear_growth (J_E=O(E)). That would be a genuinely new rule-30 theorem, but it needs a new idea for controlling the right half.

result.angle: generalize Jen: weakest right-column hypothesis that still contradicts the left edge via left-permutive reconstruction, and whether the right half driven by an eventually periodic center column satisfies it
result.summary:
Notation: c is column 0 (the center), d is column 1, e = c OR d (Lean: orCol 0), L is column -1.

**The weakest hypothesis.** Left-permutive reconstruction uses column i+1 only through orCol_i = col_i OR col_{i+1}. I proved a chain of hypotheses, each weaker than Jen's, and each still gives a contradiction. All are proved in Lean.
- (H1) c eventually periodic and e eventually periodic. Given c eventually periodic, H1 holds exactly when L is eventually periodic.
- (H2) c has period P from T, and for some n ≥ T+P, column 1 has no P-defect at the zeros of c inside [n, 2n).
- (H3) No periodicity at all: two times t1 < t2 whose (c, e) windows of length t2 coincide.

Consequences:
- **Defects in every doubling window.** If c is eventually P-periodic, column 1 breaks period P at a zero of c inside every interval [n, 2n). So there are at least about log2 N such defects below N, and finite exceptions, or exceptions with infinitely many gaps of ratio above 2, are ruled out.
- **Finitary Jen.** Columns 0 and 1 are never both P-periodic on [n-P, 2n].
- **Finite-state transducer.** If e (or d) is produced from c by a finite-state transducer, c is not eventually periodic.
- **The doubling scale is sharp.** Defects placed exactly at powers of two make every window comparison differ (checked numerically).
- **Nothing more comes from the left side.** Any pair (c, d) extends uniquely to a rule-30 field on positions p ≤ 1. The only extra fact is that this field vanishes at time 0 to the left of 0, and its consequences that do not depend on the prefix are exactly the window inequalities (H3).

**The right half driven by an eventually periodic c.**
- **Nine ones force the next two cells.** If a column is black for 9 consecutive steps, then one step later the next column to the right is white and the one after it is black. This is a check over the 2^11 states of the light cone, kernel-verified in Lean, and it held at all 7,709 occurrences in a 1,500-step run of the true pattern.
- **Long black runs exclude periodicity.** Combined with H1: no column of rule 30 is eventually periodic if, from some time on, every black run followed by a white cell has length ≥ 9. Equivalently, an eventually periodic center column must have black runs of length 1 to 8 followed by white in every period. A finitary version also holds: a P-periodic stretch with long black runs that starts at time a is shorter than a + 4P + 20. For these drivers column 1 itself is numerically not eventually periodic (for example 0 1^7 and 0 1^9). So the weakened hypothesis is genuinely needed.
- **Strip certificates.** A sound adversarial-strip method is formalised in Lean with bitmask sets. It excludes 0 1^7 and a table of 30 words of length 8–13, for every transient.
- **Scale of the classification.** Among Lyndon words of length 8–16, the e-criterion certifies 1+0+1+3+4+12+13+23+28 words beyond the 1+0+2+4+5+9+17+29+40 that the column-1 criterion certifies (strip width K ≤ 11, C code). Nothing of length 2–7 or 9 is certified.
- **Where it fails.** For 01, 001, 011, 01111 and the other words of length 2–7 and 9, e is numerically chaotic. Its defect density is 0.10–0.21 per step, the largest ratio between consecutive defects is ≤ 1.23, and the strip limit sets have both column-1 values in one cyclic class up to K = 17. So H1 and H2 fail, and the Jen-type method cannot exclude any whole period P ≥ 2.

**Lean file.** `/Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30prize/generalize-jen/Rule30JenWindow.lean` (876 lines). It compiles in about 25 s with `lake env lean` from `ruliology-lean` and uses only the axioms propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice.

claims.statement: Determination lemma. Let orCol_i(t) := cell(t,i) OR cell(t,i+1). For any column i, times t1,t2 and m: if cell(t1+s,i)=cell(t2+s,i) for 0<=s<=m and orCol_i(t1+s)=orCol_i(t2+s) for 0<=s<m, then cell(t1+s,i-k)=cell(t2+s,i-k) whenever s+k<=m. So cell(t,i-m) is a function of column i on [t,t+m] and orCol_i on [t,t+m). Column i+1 enters only at times where column i is white.
claims.proof: Rule 30 is left-permutive: (1) cell(t,j-1) = cell(t+1,j) xor orCol_j(t). Also (2) orCol_{j-1}(t) = cell(t,j-1) OR cell(t,j). Induct on k. Invariant: A_k(s) says column i-k agrees at times t1+s, t2+s (for s+k<=m), and B_k(s) says orCol_{i-k} agrees (for s+k<m). k=0 is the hypothesis. A_{k+1}(s) (needs s+k+1<=m) follows from (1) applied with j=i-k, using A_k(s+1) and B_k(s). B_{k+1}(s) follows from (2), using A_{k+1}(s) and A_k(s). QED
claims.lean_plan: Done: Rule30JenWindow.determine (with cell_left' := Rule30Jen.cell_left).

claims.statement: Window form of Jen (H3), with no periodicity hypothesis. For all t1<t2 it is impossible that c(t1+s)=c(t2+s) for all s<=t2 and orCol_0(t1+s)=orCol_0(t2+s) for all s<t2. Here c = column 0. More generally, for column i and m with i-m=-t2, the (column i, orCol_i) windows of length m at t1 and t2 differ.
claims.proof: Apply C1 with i=0, m=k=t2 and s=0: cell(t1,-t2)=cell(t2,-t2). Since -t2<-t1, cell(t1,-t2)=0 (outside the light cone, Rule30Jen.cell_eq_false_of_lt). And cell(t2,-t2)=1 (left edge, cell_left_edge). Contradiction. The column-i version is identical, with i-m=-t2. QED
claims.lean_plan: Done: window_jen, window_jen_col.

claims.statement: Periodic window form (H2). If c(t+P)=c(t) for all t>=T (P>0), then for every n>=T+P there is s in [n,2n) with c(s)=0 and d(s)!=d(s-P), where d = column 1. Corollaries: (a) there are at least floor(log2(N/(T+P))) such P-defects below N. (b) Suppose d agrees, at the zeros of c, with an eventually Q-periodic sequence outside an exceptional set S. If, with P'=lcm(P,Q), S misses [n-P',2n) for arbitrarily large n, there is a contradiction. This covers S finite, and S with infinitely many gaps s_{k+1}>2s_k+2P'.
claims.proof: Suppose no such s exists. Apply C2 with t1=n-P and t2=n. The column-0 windows agree because c is P-periodic from n-P>=T. For the orCol windows at times n-P+s and n+s (s<n): if c(n+s)=1, both ORs are 1. If c(n+s)=0, the assumption gives d(n+s)=d(n+s-P). Contradiction. (a) The disjoint intervals [2^j(T+P), 2^{j+1}(T+P)) each contain a defect. (b) Take n large with S∩[n-P',2n)=∅. Then e is P'-periodic on [n-P',2n), so the window [n,2n) has no P'-defect, contradicting the main statement for P'. QED
claims.lean_plan: Done: periodic_window. Corollaries (a) and (b) are one-line consequences (not formalised).

claims.statement: Finitary Jen. For 0<P<=n, the center column and orCol_0 are never both P-periodic on the whole interval [n-P,2n]. In particular columns 0 and 1 are never both P-periodic there.
claims.proof: C2 with t1=n-P, t2=n. The needed window equalities are exactly the periodicity relations on [n-P,2n]. QED
claims.lean_plan: Done: finitary_jen.

claims.statement: Weakened Jen (H1). If column i is eventually periodic, then orCol_i = col_i OR col_{i+1} is not eventually periodic. So column i+1 is not eventually periodic even when restricted to the times where column i is white. Moreover, given column i eventually periodic, orCol_i is eventually periodic if and only if column i-1 is. For the center: c eventually periodic implies e = c OR d is not, and L (column -1) and e determine each other via L(t)=c(t+1) xor e(t).
claims.proof: col_{i-1}(t) = col_i(t+1) xor orCol_i(t) by left-permutivity. If col_i and orCol_i are both eventually periodic, they have a common start T and period P (Rule30Jen.common_period). Then col_{i-1} is P-periodic from T, contradicting Jen's adjacent case not_adjacent(i-1). The converse direction is orCol_i(t) = col_i(t+1) xor col_{i-1}(t). QED (The center version is also proved via C3.)
claims.lean_plan: Done: or_not_eventuallyPeriodic (center, via periodic_window) and or_not_eventuallyPeriodic_col (any column, via not_adjacent).

claims.statement: Finite-state transducer form. Suppose e = c OR d (or d itself) is the output of a finite-state transducer reading column 0: e(t)=lambda(q_t,c(t)), q_{t+1}=delta(q_t,c(t)), with finitely many states. More generally, e(t) may be any function of a finite-state summary of c's past and a bounded future window of c. Then c is not eventually periodic. 'Column 1 eventually periodic up to finitely many exceptions' is a special case.
claims.proof: If c is P-periodic from T, the states q_{T+jP} (j>=0) take finitely many values. Pick j1<j2 with q_{T+j1 P}=q_{T+j2 P}. By induction on t, the pair (q_t,c(t)) is periodic with period (j2-j1)P from T+j1 P, so e is eventually periodic, contradicting C5. A bounded future window of a periodic c is itself periodic. Finitely many exceptions do not affect eventual periodicity. QED
claims.lean_plan: Not formalised. It needs a Fintype pigeonhole like Rule30Jen.pigeonhole; about 60 lines.

claims.statement: Forcing lemma. In the rule-30 pattern, if cell(t+s,j)=1 for s=0..8 (nine consecutive black cells in column j), then cell(t+9,j+1)=0 and cell(t+9,j+2)=1. Eight ones are not enough. Related exhaustive light-cone facts: the column-j blocks 011000 and 11111111 force cell(.,j+1) OR cell(.,j+2) = 1 at the next time.
claims.proof: By the light cone, cells (t+9,j+1) and (t+9,j+2) depend only on column j at times t..t+8 and on cell(t,j+1..j+11). Formally: rowList t j n = [cell t (j+1),...,cell t (j+n)], and stepList a advances such a row one step with left neighbour a, so stepList (cell t j) (rowList t j (n+1)) = rowList (t+1) j n. Iterating nine times with a=true maps rowList t j 11 to rowList (t+9) j 2. An exhaustive check over all 2^11 Boolean lists of length 11 shows that 9 steps next to a black column always end in [false,true] (kernel decide over Rule30Jen.allLists 11). QED. Sharpness: after 8 ones, 28 of the 512 light-cone states give cell(t+8,j+1)=1. The two related facts are exhaustive light-cone checks in C/Python (not in Lean).
claims.evidence: Proved in Lean, and also checked on the true pattern: 7,709 occurrences of nine vertical ones in all columns over 1,500 steps, 0 violations. The block 011000 had 7,559 occurrences and 1^8 had 3,437, with 0 violations (700 steps).
claims.lean_plan: Done: nine_ones (via nine_ones_check by decide +kernel, step_rowList, stepsTrue_rowList).

claims.statement: Long black runs exclude periodicity. Suppose that for some T, for every column i and every u>=T: if cell(u+9,i)=0 and cell(u+8,i)=1, then cell(u+s,i)=1 for all s<9. That is, from T on every black run followed by white has length >=9. Then column i is not eventually periodic. For the center: an eventually periodic center column has, in every period, a black run of length 1..8 followed by a white cell. Any period block whose cyclic black runs all have length >=9 is excluded for every transient. Finitary version: if n>=a+2P+10, the center column cannot, on all of [a,2n], be P-periodic, contain a 1 in every length-P window, and have all its black runs followed by white of length >=9. So such a stretch starting at time a has length < a+4P+20.
claims.proof: Let c = column i, d = column i+1, f = column i+2. If c is eventually 0, Rule30Prize.no_column_eventually_constant gives the contradiction. Otherwise let c have period P from T0. Then every window [t,t+P) with t>=T0 contains a 1. Fix x>=B:=T+T0+P+10. If c(x)=1 then orCol_i(x)=1. If c(x)=0, let k be the number of zeros before x in its white run: c(x-j)=0 for j<=k and c(x-k-1)=1. The window [x-P,x) contains a 1, so k<P. The run starts at r=x-k>=T+11. The hypothesis at u=r-9 gives c(r-9..r-1)=1, and C7 then gives d(r)=0, f(r)=1. If k=0, d(x)=0. If k>=1, then d(r+1)=c(r) xor (d(r) OR f(r)) = 0 xor 1 = 1, and while c=0 we have d(y+1)=d(y) OR f(y), so d stays 1 and d(x)=1. Hence orCol_i(x)=c(x) OR not c(x-1) for all x>=B. This is P-periodic, contradicting C5. Finitary version: the same argument inside [a,2n] gives orCol_0(x)=c(x) OR not c(x-1) for x in [a+P+10,2n]. Then the windows at n-P and n agree, contradicting C2. QED
claims.evidence: Column 1 is genuinely not eventually periodic for such drivers. Simulating the right half driven by 0 1^7, 0 1^9 and 0 1^12 from the true rule-30 right half at T=30, 200 and 400 gives e periodic from the start, while d is aperiodic with P-defect density 4–36%. So classical Jen (columns 0, 1) could not give these exclusions.
claims.lean_plan: Done: col_in_white_run', not_eventuallyPeriodic_of_long_one_runs_col (any column), not_eventuallyPeriodic_of_long_one_runs (center), finitary_long_runs.

claims.statement: Sound strip certificates. Encode the strip cells (t,1..K) as r<2^K. A step uses left boundary c(t) and an unknown right boundary in {0,1}; reachable sets are bitmasks. Let S0 be the set reached from all 2^K states after k periods of the word w. Suppose, at every white phase phi of w, column 1 (bit 0) is constant on the image of S0 under w[0..phi). Then the center column is not eventually equal to w repeated, in any phase and for any transient. Instances proved this way: w=01111111 (K=5, k=2 suffices; the file uses k=4), and a table of 30 words of length 8–13 (K<=9). The table contains 0111111111, 00111111111, 01011111111, 01111111111, 000111111111, 001111111111, 010111111111, 011111111111, 0000000101111, 0000111111111, 0001011111111, 0001111111111, 0010111111111, 0011111111101, 0011111111111, 0101111111111, 0110111111111, 0111111111111, 0000000011, 0011111111, 00000000001, 00000000011, 000000000001, 000000000011, 0000000000001, 0000000000011, 0000000000101, 0000000001011, 0000000010011 and 01111111.
claims.proof: Let sigma_t be the actual strip at time t (Enc K t 0 sigma_t, from encRow). Then sigma_{t+1} = stripStep K (c t) (cell t (K+1)) sigma_t (enc_step, proved bitwise with Nat.testBit lemmas), so sigma_t in S implies sigma_{t+1} in image K (c t) S (mem_imageAux). If c(t)=w[(t-T) mod P] for t>=T, then sigma_{T+kP} lies in S0. Images are monotone (imageAux_mono, applyWord_mono), and the certificate checks applyWord w S0 ⊆ S0, so by induction sigma_{T+mP} lies in S0 for all m>=k. At a white phase phi, sigma_{T+mP+phi} lies in applyWord (w.take phi) S0, on which bit 0 = cell(.,1) is a constant b_phi. Hence orCol_0(t) = w[phi] OR b_phi is eventually P-periodic, contradicting C5. The certificates are checked by decide +kernel. QED
claims.lean_plan: Done: not_eventually_word_strip, not_eventually_01111111, certTable / certTable_ok / not_eventually_certTable (about 19 s of kernel time; K>=10 entries cost too much and were left out). Generator: certgen.py (a Python mirror of stripCert). The list-based light-cone versions (forcing, not_eventually_word) are kept too.

claims.statement: Lyndon words certified by the adversarial-strip criterion at width K in {8,11}. The criterion counts as satisfied when, in the step graph of the limit sets, column 1 is a function of the cyclic class within every nontrivial strongly connected component. It is applied at white phases only (E, the weakened Jen) or at all phases (D, classical Jen). Counts (E&D / E-only / total) by length: 1: 2/0/2; 2–7: 0/0 of 1,2,3,6,9,18; 8: 1/1/30; 9: 0/0/56; 10: 2/1/99; 11: 4/3/186; 12: 5/4/335; 13: 9/12/630; 14: 17/13/1161; 15: 29/23/2182; 16: 40/28/4080. The e-weakening roughly doubles the excluded set (E-only words mostly have long 1-runs; E&D words are mostly low-density, like 0^a 1). Most certified words are 'forced' (column 1 constant per white phase), which C9 formalises. Shortest E-only word: 01111111.
claims.proof: Soundness of the criterion: the real strip trajectory is a path in the adversarial step graph (the real column K+1 is one choice of the free input). It eventually stays inside the limit sets and then inside a single strongly connected component. There the phase class advances by one each step, so column 1 at white phases is eventually periodic, and C5 applies. Only the 30 table words (and 0 1^k for k>=9, by C8) are kernel-checked. The rest are outputs of unverified C code (c/strip_scc.c, scc_scan_chunk.py; results in s11.txt..s16.txt).
claims.evidence: generalize-jen/c/strip_scc.c, scc_scan_chunk.py and s11..s16.txt. Spot checks from the true rule-30 states agree: certified words become e-periodic within a few periods.

claims.statement: The left side contains no information beyond the window inequalities. For any sequences c,d: N->{0,1} there is a unique field F on {(t,p): p<=1} with F(.,0)=c, F(.,1)=d and the rule-30 relation F(t+1,p)=F(t,p-1) xor (F(t,p) OR F(t,p+1)) for all p<=0. It depends on d only through e = c OR d. F is the true pattern (given that d is the true column 1) iff F(0,p)=0 for all p<0. So 'contradiction with the left edge via left-permutive reconstruction' means exactly that this time-0 condition fails. The consequences that do not depend on the unknown prefix c[0,T) are obtained by comparing two shifted windows (C2/H3). Additional known cells, such as the eventually periodic left diagonals, only shorten those windows by O(1).
claims.proof: Define F(t,p) for p<=-1 by recursion on -p: F(t,p)=F(t+1,p+1) xor (F(t,p+1) OR F(t,p+2)). Rearranging the xor gives the rule-30 relation at every (t+1,p) with p<=0. Any field satisfying the relation satisfies this recursion, which gives uniqueness, and the recursion uses column 1 only inside F(t,0) OR F(t,1). The true pattern is such a field. Conversely, if F(0,p)=0 for p<0, then F and the true pattern agree on row 0 for p<=1 and on column 1. The left part (p<=0) at time t+1 is determined by the left part and column 1 at time t, so by induction on t they coincide. QED

claims.statement: Failure for the chaotic core. The right half driven by an eventually periodic c does NOT, in general, satisfy the weakened hypotheses H1 or H2. For every Lyndon word of length 2–7 or 9 (and for 01, 001, 011, 0001, 0011, 0111 up to K=17), the strip criterion fails: some cyclic class of the limit sets carries both values of column 1 at a white phase. For 01 the limit sets grow roughly like 2^{0.66K} (694 states at K=10, 4873 at K=14, 19074 at K=17). For the actual driven right halves (true rule-30 right half at T=30 and 300, all phases, 16000 steps), e has P-defect density 0.214 per step (01), about 0.10 (001), about 0.12 (011) and 0.17–0.20 (01111). The largest ratio of consecutive defects is <=1.07, 1.12, 1.18 and 1.23 respectively. So H2, and a fortiori H1, fail on every window tested. Consequently no whole period P>=2 is excluded by Jen-type or strip methods. Every P<=16 has an uncertified Lyndon word of length dividing P (01 for even P; for prime P=11 or 13 more than 95% of words are uncertified).
claims.proof: The statement that e is not eventually periodic for these drivers is conjectural; proving any aperiodicity in rule 30 is of Problem-1 difficulty. What is rigorous is the method-failure part for K<=17 (finite computation, unverified C) and C11, which shows the left side cannot supply anything beyond window comparisons, and chaotic e of positive entropy satisfies all of those. Mechanism: for 01, e(t) = not(e_1(t-2) OR col2(t-1)) at white times, with e_1 = d OR col2. This dependency chain into columns 2, 3, … never closes inside a bounded strip (no forcing block exists for that phase). For words with long black runs, by contrast, C7 closes it after 9 steps.
claims.evidence: generalize-jen/defects.py, scan.py and strip_scc runs. In scans of all Lyndon words of length <=8, d and e had identical eventual-periodicity status in every run except 01111111.

claims.statement: Sharpness remarks. (a) Threshold 9 in C8: 0 1^7 is excluded (C9, via the 12-block 1111 0 1111111), but 0 1^8 is not certified for any K<=17, and numerically e is aperiodic for it. So 9 cannot be lowered to 8 within this method. (b) Doubling scale in C3: take c=(01)^infinity and e = periodic xor indicator of S at white times, with S={2^k}. Then for all 4<=t2<=700 and all t1<t2 of equal parity the e-windows of length t2 differ, so no window comparison yields a contradiction. With S={2*3^k}, equal windows exist for 365 values of t2.
claims.proof: (a) is a computation (strip_scc for 011111111 at K=11,14,17; simulation one_zero.py). (b) is a computation (pow2_windows.py) plus the following argument for S={2^k}. If e[t1,t1+t2)=e[t2,2t2), the unique power 2^a in [t2,2t2) must match a unique power 2^b in [t1,t1+t2) with 2^a-2^b=t2-t1. That forces a=b+1, and then 2^{b-1} also lies in [t1,t1+t2), a contradiction for large t2.

claims.statement: Exact light-cone forcing statistics. The fraction of column-0 blocks u of length n such that cell(t+n,1) is the same for every right-half state is: 0 for n<=6, then 2/128, 6/256, 22/512, 60/1024, 146/2048, 354/4096, 800/8192, 1770/16384, 3846/32768, 8172/65536 (12.5%) for n=7..16. Forcing blocks come in pairs u0, u1, because what is actually forced is e_1 = d OR col2. Conjecture: the density tends to a limit strictly below 1, about 0.15–0.25. So for a random-looking period block, all white phases are forced with probability exponentially small in the number of white phases.
claims.proof: Exhaustive computation with c/forcing.c: reachable-set DFS with K=n+1 cells, exact for horizon n. Minimal forcing blocks are listed in c/forcing16.txt (1166 of length <=16). The shortest are 0110000->1 and 0110001->0.

claims.statement: Generalized evidence. For every finite seed of width W<=19 (both end cells black; about 5.2e5 seeds) run 2000 steps, and for W<=10 run 16000 steps: no column in [-12,W+11] (resp. [-16,W+15]) is eventually periodic with period <=N/4 on [N/2,N). Conjecture: for every finite nonzero seed, no column of rule 30 is eventually periodic. All results here (C2–C9) are seed-independent, since they use only the left edge, left-permutivity and local forcing. This search found no seed that would show seed-independent methods to be insufficient.

claims.statement: Conjecture (partially proved): the words 0^a 1 for all a>=10 and 0^a 11 for all a>=9 are excluded for every transient. Certified individually for a<=15 (K=8, k=2 and K=6, k=2), and for a=10,11,12 (0^a 1) and a=9,10,11 (0^a 11) inside the Lean table. Sketch of a uniform proof for 0^a 1 with a>=11: in steady state (d,f,g)=(1,0,1) at each 1-time t1. Then d(t1+1)=d(t1+2)=0, f(t1+2)=1 and d=1 on [t1+3,t1+a+1]. Nine ones in column 1 (C7 applied to column 1) restore (f,g)=(0,1) at the next 1-time. The missing piece is the entry into steady state from an arbitrary state, where the switch time can be late.
claims.proof: Individual cases are proved by C9 certificates (kernel-checked for a<=12 or 13 within the table; certgen.py finds them for a<=15). The uniform steady-state propagation is the computation in the statement and is rigorous. The convergence to steady state for all a is not proved.

result.failed_approaches:
1. Plain e-weakening for short words. For every Lyndon word of length <=8 except 01111111, the driven right half had d and e with the same eventual-periodicity status in all runs: 3 true-rule-30 initial times × all phases, 2500–6000 steps, scan.py. So 'column 1 periodic only at the zeros of c' alone excludes nothing new for periods 2–7.

2. Adversarial strips at larger width. The step-graph criterion (forced, or a function of the cyclic class within each strongly connected component) up to K=17 fails for 01, 001, 011, 0001, 0011 and 0111. 0001, 0011 and 0111 are numerically absorbing for column 1 from true states but are not certifiable this way.

3. Sparse-exception versions (H2). On real driven right halves the P-defects of e have density 0.1–0.2 and consecutive-defect ratios <=1.23. No doubling gap ever appears, so the window theorem gives nothing for chaotic words.

4. Two-sided local strips, i.e. also modelling the left half next to column 0. They add nothing: by C11, every (c,d) extends uniquely to a valid left field. The left side contributes only its finite support, which is exactly the window condition.

5. Single-block light-cone forcing as a general tool. Only 12.5% of length-16 blocks force column 1, so random-looking period blocks almost never have every white phase forced.

6. Lean engineering. The list-based light-cone certificate for 01111111 (2^13 lists × 12 steps) took about 26 s of kernel time for one word. It was replaced by the bitmask strip certificate (under 1 s for K=5). Strip widths K>=10 still cost 5+ s per word (the cost grows roughly like 4^K), so they were left out of the table.

2. Scale the certificate pipeline:

- Prove uniform families by fixed points of the reachable-set dynamics, for example 0^a 1 for all a >= 10. This combines C16's steady-state argument with a finite check that the reachable set after a long white run stabilises.

3. For Problem 1 itself, Jen-type arguments are exhausted at the level of e (C11, C12). The cleanest open target is the whole of period 2, the word 01. That needs a new invariant tying the left-driven column -1, which is Λ(c) and is fed at speed 1 from the left edge whose diagonals are eventually periodic with power-of-two periods, to the right-driven e, which is chaotic. A concrete experiment: drive both halves by (01)^∞ from the true rule-30 states at many T. Then look for a statistic, such as 2-adic or diagonal-period structure, or GF(2) parity functionals like the brief's c(t) = parity #{…} identity, that the left-driven column -1 must satisfy but c(t+1) xor e(t) provably cannot.

result.angle: Algebra over GF(2). I compared rule 30 with the linear rules (60, 90, 102, 150) and with its mirror/complement (86, 135, 149). I looked at the 2-adic (Lucas/Mahler) structure of the diagonals, the algebraic normal form (ANF) and Walsh spectrum of the t-step center map Phi_t, linear complexity and generating functions, and "local algebraic forcing" (does a periodic center force a neighboring column to be periodic, which Jen's theorem forbids?). result.summary:
I did not prove Problem 1, and I did not exclude any period P >= 2 for all transients. What I did get is rigorous structure, three Lean-checked results, and several barriers that rule out whole classes of proof attempts.

Rigorous results:

(1) Right-diagonal periods are read off rows at times 2^e (Lean: R_period_iff). The diagonals R_0..R_J all have period dividing 2^e if and only if row 2^e ends with J white cells before its right-edge cell. Consequence: exact self-similar copies of early rows appear at the right end of later rows. In right-edge coordinates rule 30 is an isometry, and the closure of the single-seed orbit is the 2-adic odometer.

(2) Barrier (Lean): rules 90, 150 and 210 share every feature exploited so far, yet their single-seed centers are eventually periodic (90 and 210: 1,0,0,...; 150: all 1). The shared features are: form l xor g(c,r) with g(0,0)=0, left-permutive, two-sided light cone, Jen's argument, and 2-power-periodic right diagonals forming an odometer. So any proof must use the OR in rule 30 specifically.

(3) Lean: from a single white cell on a black background, rule 30's center column is column -1 of the usual pattern, delayed one step. By Jen, the center column is aperiodic from a single black cell, or from a single white cell, or both. Equivalently, Problem 1 holds for rule 30 or for rule 135 (whose center is the complemented, delayed column -1).

(4) Exact ANF degree (complete paper proof): for t >= 2, the center cell after t steps has degree exactly 2t-1 as a function of the 2t+1 initial cells. For t >= 3 its unique top monomial is x_{-t+2}...x_t. But degree is uninformative here: all 34 ECAs of maximal degree have eventually periodic single-seed centers.

(5) Lucas/Mahler algebra of the right diagonals, including exact linear complexities at period jumps.

(6) Local lemma for period 2: if the center reads 101010 on times [t-1, t+4], then cell(t,-4) = 0. So excluding period 2 for every transient reduces to showing that column -4 is black infinitely often at both even and odd times.

Experiments:
- Berlekamp-Massey linear complexity of c stays within 9.5 of n/2 up to n = 10^6, which forces T+P >= 499,998 for any eventual period.
- No finite seed of width <= 14 gives an eventually periodic column.
- All 2-kernel subsequences are distinct up to K = 13.
- Local forcing automata exclude nothing for periods 2 to 5.
- Right-half absorption happens, from random states, for all 3 primitive period-4 words and many words of period 8 and 10-12, but for no word of period 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 or 9. So the absorbing-word route cannot reach those periods.

arXiv 2604.00165 has no usable result: it treats rule 22, explicitly obtains no non-periodicity result, and the Theorem 2 argument as stated relies on a false XOR lemma (the second, combinatorial argument is fine).

claims.statement: Let R_j(t) = cell(t, t-j). For all e, J >= 0: (for all j <= J and all t, R_j(t+2^e) = R_j(t)) if and only if (cell(2^e, 2^e - j) = 0 for all 1 <= j <= J). Let z_e be the length of the white run immediately left of the right-edge cell in row 2^e. Then R_0..R_J all have period dividing 2^e iff J <= z_e. Also cell(t + m*2^e, p + m*2^e) = cell(t,p) whenever 0 <= t-p <= z_e and m >= 0. In particular, for 2s <= z_e, row 2^e+s ends with 0^(z_e-2s) followed by an exact copy of row s, and column 2^e reproduces c(0..z_e) at times 2^e..2^e+z_e.
claims.proof: Accumulator lemma: if x(t+1) = x(t) xor g(t) and g(t+L) = g(t) for all t, then x(t+L) = x(t) xor x(L) xor x(0) for all t. Proof by induction on t: going from t to t+1, both sides change by g(t+L) = g(t). Diagonal facts (Rule30Diagonals.lean): R_0 = 1 identically; R_1(t+1) = R_1(t) xor 1; R_{j+2}(t+1) = R_{j+2}(t) xor (R_{j+1}(t) or R_j(t)); and R_j(0) = cell(0,-j) = 0 for j >= 1. (=>) R_j(2^e) = R_j(0) = 0, and R_j(2^e) = cell(2^e, 2^e - j). (<=) Paired induction on j <= J. Case j=0 is trivial. Case j=1: apply the accumulator with g = 1 constant, so R_1(t+2^e) = R_1(t) xor R_1(2^e) xor R_1(0) = R_1(t). Case j+2: by the hypothesis the input R_{j+1} or R_j is 2^e-periodic, so R_{j+2}(t+2^e) = R_{j+2}(t) xor R_{j+2}(2^e) xor R_{j+2}(0) = R_{j+2}(t). The statement about z_e is the theorem with J ranging over [0, z_e]. The copy statement iterates the periodicity m times, since cell(t+m*2^e, p+m*2^e) = R_{t-p}(t+m*2^e). Kernel-checked as R_period_iff and right_end_copy in /Users/swish/.claude/jobs/b8cd2926/tmp/r30prize/gf2-algebra/lean/Rule30DiagonalPeriods.lean (axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; no sorry).

claims.statement: In right-edge coordinates rule 30 is an isometry, and the single-seed orbit closure is the 2-adic odometer. Define G on {0,1}^N by G(y)_j = y_j xor (y_{j-1} or y_{j-2}), with y_{-1} = y_{-2} = 0. Then G is a bijective isometry for the metric d(y,y') = 2^-min{j : y_j != y'_j}. Also G^t(e_0) = (R_j(t))_j. The map psi(alpha)_j = R_j(alpha mod 2^{e_j}) is a homeomorphism from Z_2 onto the closure of {G^t(e_0)}, and it conjugates alpha -> alpha+1 to G. The same holds verbatim for every rule l xor g(c,r) with g(0,0) = 0 whose right-diagonal periods are unbounded, including rules 60, 90, 150 and 210.
claims.proof: G is triangular: G(y)_j = y_j xor h(y_0..y_{j-1}). So it is invertible (solve for y_j inductively). If y and y' first differ at index n, then G(y) and G(y') agree below n and differ at n, so G preserves d exactly. G^t(e_0) = R(t) is the diagonal recurrence. Each R_j is purely periodic with period 2^{e_j}, so psi is well defined and continuous on Z_2. psi(t) = R(t) on N, and psi(alpha+1) = G(psi(alpha)) holds on the dense set N, hence everywhere by continuity. Injectivity: the truncation of G to the first J+1 coordinates is well defined. The truncated orbit of e_0 is periodic with least period 2^{E_J}, where E_J = max_{i<=J} e_i, and the points of a periodic orbit within one period are pairwise distinct. So psi(alpha) = psi(beta) forces alpha = beta mod 2^{E_J} for every J. E_J tends to infinity because L(R_j) > ceil(j/2) (claim C(b)). Hence alpha = beta. A continuous injection from compact Z_2 into a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image, and that image is the orbit closure. For a general g the same proof applies whenever the periods are unbounded. For rule 60 the diagonals are binomial(t,j) mod 2, with period 2^ceil(log2(j+1)). For rules 90, 150 and 210 the zero-run argument of C(b) applies. Consequence for Problem 1: the center column is the anti-diagonal c(t) = psi(t)_t, which is not a continuous observable on the odometer. Rules 90, 150 and 210 have the same odometer structure and periodic centers (claim F), so this structure alone cannot decide Problem 1.

claims.statement:
Lucas/Mahler structure. Every 2^e-periodic u: N -> GF(2) has a unique expansion u(t) = sum_{m<2^e} mu_m binomial(t,m) mod 2, with mu_m = sum over k with bits(k) contained in bits(m) of u(k). Its linear complexity is L(u) = 1 + max{m : mu_m = 1}. Lucas gives binomial(t,m)*binomial(t,m') = binomial(t, m OR m') mod 2. For the right diagonals, with L_j = L(R_j):
(a) L_j = L(R_{j-1} or R_{j-2}) + 1, and the least period is 2^{e_j} with e_j = ceil(log2 L_j).
(b) log2(ceil(j/2)+1) <= e_j <= max(e_{j-1}, e_{j-2}) + 1.
(c) If e_j > max(e_{j-1}, e_{j-2}), then L_j = 2^{e_j - 1} + 1.
(d) If moreover L_{j-1} >= 2, then L_{j+1} = 2^{e_j - 1} + L_{j-1} + 1.
claims.proof: Over GF(2), (E+1) binomial(t,m) = binomial(t,m-1) (Pascal), so Delta^k binomial(.,m) = binomial(.,m-k), and binomial(.,m) is annihilated by Delta^{m+1} but not by Delta^m. The functions binomial(t,m) mod 2 = product of t_i over i in bits(m), for m < 2^e, form a basis of the functions on Z/2^e (Mobius inversion over bit subsets). Hence the expansion is unique and L(u) = min{k : Delta^k u = 0} = 1 + (top index). Also u is 2^e-periodic iff its top index is < 2^e, so the least period is 2^ceil(log2 L). Summation: sum_{s<t} binomial(s,m) = binomial(t,m+1), so the operator S shifts every index up by 1. Since R_j = S(R_{j-1} or R_{j-2}) with R_j(0) = 0, we get L_j = L(input) + 1, which is (a). (b) Upper bound: S of a 2^a-periodic sequence is 2^(a+1)-periodic. Lower bound: R_j(t) = 0 for t < j/2 (outside the light cone), while R_j(ceil(j/2)) = 1 (left edge if j is even; second left diagonal D_1 = 1 if j is odd). A nonzero sequence annihilated by (1+E)^L cannot have L consecutive zeros, because the constant term is invertible and the recurrence runs backwards. Hence L_j > ceil(j/2). (c) The input has period dividing 2^{e-1}, so L(input) <= 2^{e-1}. Least period 2^e forces L_j > 2^{e-1}, so L_j = 2^{e-1} + 1. (d) By (c), R_j = binomial(t, 2^{e-1}) + (terms with index < 2^{e-1}). R_{j-1} has top index m* = L_{j-1} - 1, with 1 <= m* < 2^{e-1}. In R_j or R_{j-1} = R_j + R_{j-1} + R_j*R_{j-1}, a product term binomial(t,m1)*binomial(t,m2) contributes index m1 OR m2. With m1 = 2^{e-1} and m2 <= m*, this union is 2^{e-1} + m2 <= 2^{e-1} + m*, with equality only for m2 = m*. Unions of indices below 2^{e-1} stay below 2^{e-1}. So the top index of the OR is exactly 2^{e-1} + m*, with coefficient 1. Then L(OR) = 2^{e-1} + L_{j-1} and L_{j+1} = L(OR) + 1.
claims.evidence: mahler.c gives exact L_j for j <= 50. At every jump L_j = 2^{e_j - 1} + 1, e.g. L_16 = 129, L_25 = 513, L_49 = 524289. The step after a jump matches (d): L_17 = 128+65+1 = 194, L_26 = 512+257+1 = 770, L_38 = 16384+8193+1 = 24578, L_50 = 524288+262145+1 = 786434. claims.statement: Let Phi_t: GF(2)^{[-t,t]} -> GF(2) be the center cell after t steps of rule 30, as a function of the initial cells x_{-t}..x_t. For t >= 2, deg Phi_t = 2t-1 (deg Phi_1 = 2). For t >= 3, the unique monomial of degree 2t-1 is M_t = x_{-t+2} x_{-t+3} ... x_t. (The single-seed center is the linear coefficient c(t) = coef_{x_0}(Phi_t), and the degree-1 part of Phi_t is sum_p cell(t,-p) x_p.)
claims.proof:
Notation: coef_S(f) = XOR over U subset of S of f(1_U).
(F1) Left-permutivity: cell(s,q) = x_{q-s} xor (a function of x_{q-s+1..q+s}). In particular Phi_t = x_{-t} xor Psi_t(x_{-t+1..t}).
(F2) Unrolling along the right diagonal gives Phi_t = x_{-t} xor XOR_{s<t} (cell(s,s-t+1) or cell(s,s-t+2)). The variable x_{-t+1} enters cell(s,s-t+1) linearly (it is that cell's leftmost variable) and does not enter cell(s,s-t+2). Since d/da (a or b) = 1 xor b, we get d/dx_{-t+1} Phi_t = t xor XOR_{s<t} cell(s,s-t+2).
(F3) Only the cell A_s = cell(s,t-s) of the backward cone at time s depends on x_t. With B_s = cell(s,t-s-1), we have A_{s+1} = cell(s,t-s-2) xor B_s xor A_s(1 xor B_s), so d/dx_t Phi_t = product_{s<t} (1 xor cell(s,t-1-s)).
Upper bound (t >= 2): by F1, x_{-t} appears only in the monomial x_{-t}. The coefficient of the full monomial x_{-t+1}...x_t equals the full-monomial coefficient over x_{-t+2..t} of XOR_{s<t} cell(s,s-t+2) (by F2). Only s = t-1 uses all of these variables, and cell(t-1,1) = x_{-t+2} xor f(x_{-t+3..t}) has zero coefficient on every monomial of degree >= 2 containing x_{-t+2}. So that coefficient is 0, and every remaining monomial has degree <= 2t-1.
Uniqueness (t >= 3): monomials containing x_{-t+1} have degree <= 1 + max_{s<t} deg cell(s,.) <= 1 + (2t-3). This uses the upper bound for 2 <= s <= t-1, and degrees 1 and 2 for s = 0 and 1. So a degree-(2t-1) monomial avoids x_{-t} and x_{-t+1}, which leaves only M_t.
Lower bound: coef(M_t, Phi_t) = coef(x_{-t+2}...x_{t-1}, d/dx_t Phi_t). By F3 and Mobius inversion, with m = t-1, this is the parity of #{x in GF(2)^{[-m,m]} : x_{-m} = 0 and cell(s,m-s) = 0 for all 0 <= s <= m}.
Re-coordinatize by diagonals L_k(s) = cell(s, m-k-s). Rule 30 solved for the left input gives L_{k+2}(s) = L_k(s+1) xor (L_{k+1}(s) or L_k(s)). Hence base <-> (L_0(0..m), L_1(0..m-1)) is a bijection: both sets have 2^{2m+1} elements, the forward map is evaluation, and the inverse is this recursion. Under L_0 = 0, the base is a function of w = L_1 in GF(2)^m, and x_{-m} = L_{2m}(0) = f_{2m}(w). Here f_0 = 0, f_1 = w_0, f_{k+2}(w) = f_k(sigma w) xor (f_{k+1}(w) or f_k(w)), with sigma the shift. f_{2i} and f_{2i-1} depend on w_0..w_{i-1}. So the count = 2^m - wt(f_{2m}), which is congruent to wt(f_{2m}) = top(f_{2m}) mod 2.
Induction 1: f_{2j-1} = w_{j-1} xor (a function of w_0..w_{j-2}), because f_{2j-1} = f_{2j-3}(sigma w) xor (f_{2j-2} or f_{2j-3}) and the last two depend on w_0..w_{j-2}.
Induction 2, for i >= 2: f_{2i} = f_{2i-2}(sigma w) xor f_{2i-2} xor f_{2i-1}(1 xor f_{2i-2}). The first two terms miss w_0 and w_{i-1} respectively. Write f_{2i-1} = A xor B, with A = f_{2i-3}(sigma w) on w_1..w_{i-1} (permutive in w_{i-1}) and B on w_0..w_{i-2}; then B(1 xor f_{2i-2}) misses w_{i-1}. So top(f_{2i}) = sum over w of A(1 xor f_{2i-2}) = sum over w_1..w_{i-2} of (sum over w_{i-1} of A)(sum over w_0 of (1 xor f_{2i-2})) = sum over w_1..w_{i-2} of d/dw_0 f_{2i-2} = top(f_{2i-2}).
Since top(f_2) = top(w_0) = 1, the count is odd and coef(M_t) = 1.
